topic-1-1-1.foundation: 1. \(P\) (axiom). 2. \(P\) implies \(Q\) (axiom). 3. \(Q\) (modus ponens, lines 1 and 2). 4. \(Q\) implies \(R\) (axiom). 5. \(R\) (modus ponens, lines 3 and 4). Each line is either an axiom or follows from earlier lines by the rule, so a checker can verify the proof line by line.
topic-1-1-1.application: Let the even integer be \(2a\) and the odd integer \(2b+1\), with \(a\) and \(b\) integers (definitions of even and odd). Then \(2a+(2b+1)=2(a+b)+1\) (associativity and the distributive law). Since \(a+b\) is an integer, \(2(a+b)+1\) has the form of an odd integer (definition of odd). Hence the sum is odd.
topic-1-1-1.challenge: Take the axiom “every integer is even.” Applying it to \(3\) gives the line “\(3\) is even,” which the checker accepts as an instance of the axiom. The conclusion is false because the axiom is false. An accepted proof establishes only that the conclusion follows from the axioms by the rules. Whether the axioms are true, or at least consistent, is a separate question that the checker does not settle.

topic-1-1-2.foundation: No. From \(P\) and “\(P\) implies not \(P\),” modus ponens gives “not \(P\).” The system proves both \(P\) and its negation.
topic-1-1-2.application: Inconsistency means that the system proves some \(A\) and also not \(A\). Applying the rule to these two proofs gives a proof of any statement \(B\) we choose. An inconsistent system of this kind proves everything, so its theorems carry no information.
topic-1-1-2.challenge: If \(S\) is inconsistent, it proves every statement it can express, including the statement “\(S\) is consistent.” So a proof of that statement within \(S\) is exactly what an inconsistent \(S\) would also produce, and it cannot by itself show that \(S\) is consistent. This is why Hilbert sought a consistency proof using only weaker, finitary reasoning that is easier to trust than the system being justified.

topic-1-1-3.foundation: The list begins: the empty string, \(a\), \(b\), \(aa\), \(ab\), \(ba\), \(bb\). The string \(ab\) is fifth.
topic-1-1-3.application: There are \(2^k\) strings of length \(k\), so the strings of length at most \(5\) number \(1+2+4+8+16+32=63\). The search finds a proof among the first \(63\) candidates. The bound needs the length of the shortest proof, which is unknown in advance, and if no proof exists the search never stops, so no bound applies at all.
topic-1-1-3.challenge: Check candidates in turn, alternating between proofs of \(P\) and proofs of not \(P\). By completeness, one of them has a proof, so the search stops after finitely many steps. If it finds a proof of \(P\), then \(P\) is provable. If it finds a proof of not \(P\), then \(P\) is not provable, since by consistency the theory cannot prove both. The procedure always stops with the correct answer. The argument needs completeness, which fails for arithmetic by the incompleteness theorem.

topic-1-2-1.application: \(21=1\cdot13+8\), \(13=1\cdot8+5\), \(8=1\cdot5+3\), \(5=1\cdot3+2\), \(3=1\cdot2+1\), \(2=2\cdot1+0\): six divisions, and the greatest common divisor is \(1\). Every quotient but the last is \(1\), so each remainder is the difference of the two previous numbers, the smallest decrease possible. The entries run backward through the Fibonacci numbers \(21,13,8,5,3,2,1\).
topic-1-2-1.challenge: Replacing \((a,b)\) by \((b,a)\) keeps the greatest common divisor unchanged but never reduces anything, so it runs forever. Replacing \((a,b)\) by \((b,0)\) and returning \(b\) always stops, but from \((4,6)\) it returns \(6\), while the greatest common divisor is \(2\). Preserving the answer does not imply termination, and termination does not imply a correct answer. Euclid’s algorithm needs both arguments: the invariant and the decreasing second entry.

topic-1-2-2.foundation: It must record the current value \(30\), the divisor \(18\), the number of subtractions made so far, \(1\), and the fact that the computation is in the middle of a division rather than at the start of a new step. The earlier pairs need not be recorded.
topic-1-2-2.application: The run is \((30,18)\to(18,12)\to(12,6)\to(6,0)\). Any pair \((18q+12,18)\) with \(q\geq0\) gives the remainder \(12\) on division by \(18\): for example \((48,18)\) and \((66,18)\), and also \((12,18)\), for which the quotient is \(0\).
topic-1-2-2.challenge: A step sends \((a,b)\) to \((b,r)\), so we need \(b=18\) and remainder \(r=12\) on dividing \(a\) by \(18\): \(a=18q+12\) for some integer \(q\geq0\). There are infinitely many such pairs, one for each \(q\). From \((18,12)\) alone we cannot recover the previous pair; we would also need the quotient \(q\), which the algorithm discards.

topic-1-2-3.foundation: Number the cells \(1,2,3,\dots\). The configurations are: tape \(111\), head at cell \(1\), state \(q\); head at cell \(2\), state \(q\); head at cell \(3\), state \(q\); head at cell \(4\), which is blank, state \(q\); then the machine halts in state \(h\) with the head at cell \(4\). The tape never changes.
topic-1-2-3.application: It moves right over the \(n\) ones and writes a \(1\) in the first blank cell, so the block grows to \(n+1\) ones: in unary notation, it computes \(n+1\). It takes \(n\) moves and one final write, \(n+1\) steps in all.
topic-1-2-3.challenge: Use two running states, \(E\) (an even number of ones read so far) and \(O\) (odd), starting in \(E\). In \(E\) reading \(1\): move right and enter \(O\). In \(O\) reading \(1\): move right and enter \(E\). In \(E\) reading a blank: halt in “even.” In \(O\) reading a blank: halt in “odd.” On \(111\) the states are \(E\to O\to E\to O\), and the blank is read in \(O\), so the machine halts in “odd.”

topic-1-3-1.foundation: Exactly the Turing-computable functions. Both simulations are mathematical constructions between two precisely defined models, so the conclusion is a theorem. The thesis is not needed.
topic-1-3-1.application: (a) and (c) are theorems: they compare precisely defined models. (b) is the thesis: “effective mechanical method” is an informal idea, so the statement cannot be proved as a theorem about defined objects.
topic-1-3-1.challenge: Define \(f(n)=1\) if \(M_n\), run on input \(n\), halts with output \(0\), and \(f(n)=0\) otherwise. For every \(n\), \(f(n)\) differs from the output of \(M_n\) on \(n\), or \(M_n\) fails to produce \(0\) or \(1\) there. So \(f\) is computed by no machine in the list, that is, by no Turing machine. By the Church–Turing thesis, no effective mechanical method computes it either.

topic-1-3-2.foundation: (a) halts: \(x\) decreases to \(0\). (b) does not halt: \(x\) takes the values \(5,3,1,-1,\dots\) and never equals \(0\). (c) does not halt. Particular programs can often be decided by inspection; the halting theorem rules out one procedure that works for every program.
topic-1-3-2.application: A program that counts down from \(1{,}000{,}001\), one decrement per step, and then stops will outlast the test. For any fixed cutoff \(B\), a countdown longer than \(B\) gives the same counterexample. A timeout shows only that the program has not halted yet; it does not prove that it never will.
topic-1-3-2.challenge: Given \((P,x)\), let \(P^\prime\) be the program that ignores its input and runs \(P\) on \(x\). Then \(P^\prime\) halts on \(0\) exactly when \(P\) halts on \(x\), and \(P^\prime\) can be written down from \(P\) and \(x\) by an algorithm. If some algorithm decided halting on input \(0\), applying it to \(P^\prime\) would decide whether \(P\) halts on \(x\), for every pair. That would solve the halting problem, which is impossible. So no such algorithm exists.

topic-1-3-3.foundation: From \(P\) alone, modus ponens yields nothing new, so the theorems are just \(P\). Neither \(Q\) nor not \(Q\) is provable, so \(Q\) is undecided and the theory is incomplete. This toy theory is incomplete for a trivial reason: it says nothing about \(Q\).
topic-1-3-3.application: If \(T\) with \(G\) added were inconsistent, \(T\) would prove not \(G\), refuting \(G\), contrary to assumption. If \(T\) with not \(G\) added were inconsistent, \(T\) would prove not not \(G\), that is, \(G\), again contrary to assumption. So both extensions are consistent, and the axioms of \(T\) alone do not decide \(G\).
topic-1-3-3.challenge: The added axioms are produced by an algorithm, so the combined list of axioms can still be listed by an algorithm: list the original axioms and run the extension procedure, interleaving the two. The combined theory is therefore effectively axiomatized, contains arithmetic, and is consistent by assumption. The incompleteness theorem applies to it, so it too leaves some sentence undecided. Adding axioms by any algorithm can never reach completeness.

topic-1-4-1.foundation: It is deterministic: each configuration has exactly one successor. \(B\) has two predecessors, \(A\) and \(D\), and \(A\) has none. The rule is not reversible.
topic-1-4-1.application: From \(A\): \(A,B,C,D,B,C,D\), ending at \(D\). From \(B\): \(B,C,D,B,C,D,B\), ending at \(B\). From \(C\), the run ends at \(C\), and from \(D\) at \(D\). The runs from \(A\) and from \(D\) both end at \(D\), so the configuration after six steps does not determine where the run started.
topic-1-4-1.challenge: A one-to-one rule sends the \(N\) configurations to \(N\) different configurations, so every configuration is reached: the rule is onto. Now follow a run \(c_0,c_1,c_2,\dots\). With finitely many configurations, some configuration repeats; let \(c_i=c_j\), with \(i\lt j\) and \(i\) as small as possible. If \(i\gt 0\), then \(c_{i-1}\) and \(c_{j-1}\) have the same successor, so by one-to-oneness \(c_{i-1}=c_{j-1}\), a repeat with a smaller first index. Hence \(i=0\): the run returns to \(c_0\).

topic-1-4-2.foundation: \(x\land y\) loses information: \(00\), \(01\), and \(10\) all give \(0\). The XOR \(x\oplus y\) alone also loses it: \(00\) and \(11\) both give \(0\). The maps \((x,x\oplus y)\) and \((y,x)\) are one-to-one: \((x,x\oplus y)\) is undone by applying it again, and the swap by swapping back.
topic-1-4-2.application: The outputs are \(000\), \(010\), \(100\), and \(111\). Applying the map again gives \(t\oplus(x\land y)\oplus(x\land y)=t\), so every input is restored: the map is its own inverse, even though AND itself loses information.
topic-1-4-2.challenge: There are \(2^n\) inputs and two outputs, so by the pigeonhole principle one output is shared by at least \(2^{n-1}\) inputs. To be one-to-one, the outputs must take at least \(2^n\) different values, which needs at least \(n\) bits in total: the answer bit and at least \(n-1\) further bits. Keeping all \(n\) input bits always suffices, since the input can then be read off directly. Whether \(n-1\) kept bits are enough depends on the function.

topic-2-1-1.application: Since \(2^9=512\leq1000\lt 1024=2^{10}\), binary needs \(10\) bits, while unary needs \(1000\) marks. A procedure taking \(N\) steps is linear in the unary length but exponential in the binary length, about \(2^{10}\) steps for \(10\) bits. The same procedure is “efficient” or not depending on the encoding.
topic-2-1-1.challenge: There are \(2^n\) bit strings of length \(n\). An encoding gives different integers different strings, so it needs at least \(M\) strings: \(2^n\geq M\). Taking logarithms, \(n\geq\log_2M\). Binary achieves this up to rounding up.

topic-2-1-2.application: A truth table has four rows, each with output \(0\) or \(1\), so there are \(2^4=16\) functions. Those with a single \(1\): output \(1\) only on \(11\) (AND), only on \(10\) (\(x\) and not \(y\)), only on \(01\) (not \(x\) and \(y\)), and only on \(00\) (NOR).
topic-2-1-2.challenge: The truth table has \(2^n\) rows, and each row’s output can be chosen independently, giving \(2^{2^n}\) functions. For \(n=10\) that is \(2^{1024}\). The number of bit strings shorter than \(1014\) bits is \(1+2+\dots+2^{1013}=2^{1014}-1\lt 2^{1014}\). Different functions need different descriptions, so at most \(2^{1014}\) functions have such a short description, a fraction below \(2^{1014}/2^{1024}=2^{-10}\lt 1/1000\). Almost every function has no description much shorter than its truth table.

topic-2-1-3.foundation: It equals \(1\) only when both factors are \(1\), that is, when \(x=y=0\). For \(00,01,10,11\) the values are \(1,0,0,0\): this is NOR, the negation of OR.
topic-2-1-3.application: XOR is \(1\) on the rows \(01\) and \(10\). Their detectors are \((1+x)y\) and \(x(1+y)\), so XOR is \((1+x)y+x(1+y)=y+xy+x+xy=x+y\pmod2\), since \(xy+xy=0\).
topic-2-1-3.challenge: Majority is \(1\) on \(011\), \(101\), \(110\), and \(111\). The detectors add to \((1+x)yz+x(1+y)z+xy(1+z)+xyz=yz+xz+xy+4xyz\). Since \(4xyz=0\) modulo two, the polynomial is \(xy+yz+xz\). Check: on \(110\) it gives \(1+0+0=1\), and on \(111\) it gives \(1+1+1=1\).

topic-2-2-1.foundation: The AND gate outputs \(u=1\cdot0=0\). The first XOR gate outputs \(x+y=1\). The second XOR gate combines these: \(1+0=1\). The output is \(1\), as OR requires.
topic-2-2-1.application: Three AND gates compute \(xy\), \(yz\), and \(xz\), and two XOR gates add them: first \(xy+yz\), then that sum plus \(xz\). That is five gates in all.
topic-2-2-1.challenge: Parity is \(1\) on \(2^{n-1}\) of the \(2^n\) inputs, so the construction adds \(2^{n-1}\) detectors, each a product of \(n\) factors. After simplification the polynomial is just \(x_1+\dots+x_n\), which needs \(n-1\) XOR gates. The general construction proves that a circuit exists, but it can be exponentially wasteful.

topic-2-2-2.foundation: \(\operatorname{NAND}\) gives \(1,1,1,0\) on \(00,01,10,11\). Feeding the same bit into both inputs of a NAND gate negates it, so the outer gate turns \(1,1,1,0\) into \(0,0,0,1\), which is AND.
topic-2-2-2.application:
\(a\lor b=\operatorname{NAND}(
eg a,
eg b)\) with \(
eg a=\operatorname{NAND}(a,a)\): three gates. For \(00\): \(\operatorname{NAND}(1,1)=0\). For \(01\): \(\operatorname{NAND}(1,0)=1\). For \(10\): \(\operatorname{NAND}(0,1)=1\). For \(11\): \(\operatorname{NAND}(0,0)=1\). These are the outputs of OR.
topic-2-2-2.challenge: On the all-zero input, AND and XOR gates output \(0\) when both their inputs are \(0\). By induction along the circuit, every wire carries \(0\), so the output is \(0\); NOT must output \(1\) on input \(0\). With the constant \(1\), \(\neg x=x\oplus1\), and AND together with NOT builds NAND, which is universal.

topic-2-2-3.foundation: Output \(0\) comes only from \(00\); output \(1\) comes from \(01\), \(10\), and \(11\). After an output \(1\), the input cannot be recovered.
topic-2-2-3.application: The outputs are \(00\mapsto(0,0)\), \(01\mapsto(0,1)\), \(10\mapsto(0,1)\), and \(11\mapsto(1,1)\). The inputs \(01\) and \(10\) collide, so the map is not one-to-one, even though it produces two bits from two.
topic-2-2-3.challenge: Given the output \((x,s)\) with \(s=x\oplus y\), we recover \(y=x\oplus s\). So different inputs give different outputs. The XOR gate alone cannot distinguish \(00\) from \(11\), but the copied \(x\) separates them. The information is kept by the fan-out copy, not by the gate.

topic-2-3-1.application: \(10^{18}\times2.9\times10^{-21}\) J per second is about \(2.9\times10^{-3}\) W, roughly \(3\) mW. A \(50\) W processor dissipates more than ten thousand times this. Today’s heat comes mostly from other losses, not from the erasure limit.
topic-2-3-1.challenge: \(H=-0.9\log_20.9-0.1\log_20.1\approx0.137+0.332=0.469\). The cost is about \(0.47\,k_{\mathrm B}T\ln2\), roughly half that of an unbiased bit, for which \(H=1\). For a known bit, \(p=1\) gives \(H=0\): nothing uncertain is erased, so no minimum cost applies.

topic-2-3-2.foundation: NOT and \((x,y)\mapsto(x,x\oplus y)\) are one-to-one, hence reversible. AND and the reset merge different inputs, so they are not.
topic-2-3-2.application: No contradiction: reversibility is a property of the map, and the device may lose energy for other reasons. Landauer’s principle requires no minimum for NOT, since NOT erases nothing. The bound applies only when information is erased.
topic-2-3-2.challenge: A reversible map is one-to-one on the \(2^n\) strings, and a one-to-one map of a finite set to itself is onto, so it is a permutation. For \(n=2\) there are \(4!=24\) permutations of the four strings, while all maps number \(4^4=256\). Fewer than one map in ten is reversible.

topic-2-3-3.foundation: \(000\to000\), \(010\to011\), \(100\to101\), and \(110\to111\): the target receives the OR of the inputs.
topic-2-3-3.application: The first call gives \((1,0,0)\), since \(1\oplus1=0\). The second gives \((1,0,1)\), restoring the input. The oracle adds the function value modulo two to the existing target; it does not overwrite that target. To read \(f(x)\) directly from the target, initialize it to \(0\).
topic-2-3-3.challenge: \(U_f(U_f(x,t))=U_f(x,t\oplus f(x))=(x,t\oplus f(x)\oplus f(x))=(x,t)\), because each bit of \(f(x)\) added twice modulo two gives \(0\). So \(U_f\) undoes itself. In particular it is one-to-one, whatever \(f\) is.

topic-2-4-1.application: \((a,b)\to(a,\,a\oplus b)\to\bigl(a\oplus(a\oplus b),\,a\oplus b\bigr)=(b,\,a\oplus b)\to\bigl(b,\,b\oplus a\oplus b\bigr)=(b,a)\). Three CNOT gates swap two bits.
topic-2-4-1.challenge: The inverse keeps \(c\) and applies \(g_c^{-1}\) to the target: since \(c\) is unchanged, it knows which map to undo. If \(g_1\) resets the target to \(0\), the inputs \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\) both go to \((1,0)\), so the controlled operation is not one-to-one.

topic-2-4-2.foundation: Only those with \(a=b=1\): \(110\to111\) and \(111\to110\). The other six are unchanged.
topic-2-4-2.application: \(a\land b\): Toffoli with controls \(a,b\) and a target set to \(0\). \(\neg a\): controls set to \(1,1\) and target \(a\), giving \(a\oplus1\). \(a\oplus b\): controls \(1\) and \(a\) with target \(b\), giving \(b\oplus a\).
topic-2-4-2.challenge: Each input bit has this form. NOT adds \(1\), and CNOT replaces the target by the sum of target and control; both keep the form, so by induction along the circuit every bit has it. If \(a\land b=c_0+c_1a+c_2b\) modulo two, the input \(00\) gives \(c_0=0\), the input \(10\) gives \(c_1=0\), and \(01\) gives \(c_2=0\), but then \(11\) gives \(0\neq1\).

topic-2-4-3.foundation: \((1,1,0,0,0)\to(1,1,0,1,0)\to(1,1,0,1,0)\to(1,1,0,0,0)\). The second gate does nothing because \(z=0\), so \(t=0=1\land1\land0\), and the third gate resets \(w\).
topic-2-4-3.application: 1. Controls \(x,y\), target \(w_1\): \(w_1=xy\). 2. Controls \(w_1,z\), target \(w_2\): \(w_2=xyz\). 3. Controls \(w_2,u\), target \(t\): \(t=xyzu\). 4. Repeat gate 2, resetting \(w_2\). 5. Repeat gate 1, resetting \(w_1\). The uncomputation runs in reverse order, because gate 2 needs \(w_1\) to still hold \(xy\).
topic-2-4-3.challenge: \(A\) gives \((x,f(x),g(x);0)\). The CNOT gates add \(f(x)\) into the fresh register, giving \((x,f(x),g(x);f(x))\) and leaving the first three registers unchanged. \(A^{-1}\) acts only on those three; since \(A(x,0,0)=(x,f(x),g(x))\), it returns them to \((x,0,0)\). The result is \((x,0,0;f(x))\).

topic-3-1-1.foundation: (a) \(v_{10}=1\) and the other three weights are \(0\). (b) \(v_{10}=v_{11}=1\), and \(v_{00}=v_{01}=0\): these weights record which configurations are possible. (c) Each configuration has probability \(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14\), so all four weights are \(1/4\).
topic-3-1-1.application: Probabilities of the two configurations must add to \(1\), and these add to \(2\), so they are not probabilities. They record that both values are possible and nothing more: they say nothing about how often each occurs. The states with \(v_0=v_1=1/2\) and with \(v_0=1/10\), \(v_1=9/10\) are both consistent with them, as is any pair of positive probabilities adding to \(1\).
topic-3-1-1.challenge: There are \(2^k\) configurations, and a possibility state is fixed by the set of configurations with weight \(1\). Any nonempty set will do, so there are \(2^{2^k}-1\) possibility states. Probability states are infinitely many: any nonnegative weights adding to \(1\) give one, and they vary continuously. A probability state is consistent with “every configuration is possible” exactly when every one of its weights is positive. The possibility state keeps only which weights are nonzero.

topic-3-1-2.foundation: The diagram has three circles and the arrows \(0\to1\), \(1\to2\), \(2\to0\), each with weight \(1\). The run from \(0\) is \(0,1,2,0,1\): the configuration returns to \(0\) every three steps.
topic-3-1-2.application: Each of the two steps, from \(t=0\) to \(1\) and from \(t=1\) to \(2\), repeats the three arrows of the rule, so the diagram has \(6\) arrows. The run from \(2\) is \(2,0,1\), the path from \(2\) at time \(0\) to \(0\) at time \(1\) to \(1\) at time \(2\).
topic-3-1-2.challenge: Each of the \(t\) steps repeats the \(a\) arrows, so there are \(ta\) arrows. A run \(c_0,\dots,c_t\) uses an allowed arrow \(c_s\to c_{s+1}\) at every step, which is exactly an arrow from \(c_s\) at time \(s\) to \(c_{s+1}\) at time \(s+1\); conversely, a path from time \(0\) to time \(t\) visits one configuration at each time, joined by allowed arrows, which is a run. Every arrow of the time-expanded diagram goes from time \(s\) to time \(s+1\), so no path can return to an earlier time: a cycle of the state diagram, such as RESET’s arrow \(0\to0\), becomes a chain of arrows moving forward in time.

topic-3-1-3.foundation: The run is \(01,10,01\). Exactly one arrow leaves each configuration, so SWAP is deterministic. Exactly one arrow also enters each configuration: \(00\) from \(00\), \(01\) from \(10\), \(10\) from \(01\), and \(11\) from \(11\). So SWAP is reversible; in fact, applying it twice restores every configuration, so it is its own inverse.
topic-3-1-3.application: INC has the arrows \(0\to1\to2\to3\to0\), so the run from \(3\) is \(3,0,1\). HALVE has the arrows \(0\to0\), \(1\to0\), \(2\to1\), and \(3\to1\), so the run from \(3\) is \(3,1,0\). Both are deterministic. INC is reversible: each configuration has exactly one incoming arrow, and subtracting \(1\) undoes it. HALVE is not: two arrows enter \(0\) and two enter \(1\), while none enters \(2\) or \(3\). From the end \(0\) of a run we cannot tell whether it started at \(0\), \(1\), \(2\), or \(3\).
topic-3-1-3.challenge: Suppose there are \(N\) configurations. A deterministic rule has exactly one outgoing arrow at each, so \(N\) arrows in total, and these \(N\) arrows enter the \(N\) configurations. If every configuration receives at least one, none can receive two, since that would require more than \(N\) arrows. So each receives exactly one, and the rule is reversible. Conversely, a reversible rule gives every configuration exactly one incoming arrow, hence at least one. For \(n\mapsto\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) on all nonnegative integers, every \(n\) has an incoming arrow, from \(2n\); yet \(2n\) and \(2n+1\) both go to \(n\), so the rule is not reversible. The counting argument needs finitely many configurations.

topic-3-1-4.foundation: From \(0\) the only allowed arrow is \(0\to1\); from \(1\), both \(1\to0\) and \(1\to1\) are allowed. The possible runs are \(0\to1\to0\) and \(0\to1\to1\). Both \(0\) and \(1\) are reachable at time \(2\), each by one path.
topic-3-1-4.application: Extend each two-step run by an allowed arrow. From \(0\to1\to0\), only \(0\to1\) is allowed, giving \(0\to1\to0\to1\). From \(0\to1\to1\), both arrows are allowed, giving \(0\to1\to1\to0\) and \(0\to1\to1\to1\). So \(1\) is reachable by two paths and \(0\) by one. The counts differ, but neither configuration is “more possible”: both are simply reachable.
topic-3-1-4.challenge: Each step either stays or advances by one, so reaching \(k\) needs \(k\) advances, and \(k\) is reachable at time \(t\) exactly when \(t\geq k\). Once at \(k\), every later step must stay. A path from \(0\) to \(k\) at time \(t\) is therefore fixed by choosing which \(k\) of the \(t\) steps advance: the last advance may fall anywhere, and the forced stays afterward are consistent with the choice. Every choice of \(k\) steps out of \(t\) gives exactly one allowed path, so there are \(\binom tk\) of them. The number of paths grows quickly with \(t\), but it measures only how many ways there are to reach \(k\), not how likely \(k\) is.

topic-3-1-5.foundation: Two paths end at \(0\). The path \(0\to0\to0\) has probability \((2/3)(2/3)=4/9\), and \(0\to1\to0\) has probability \((1/3)(1/3)=1/9\). They cannot both happen, so \(P(c_2=0)=4/9+1/9=5/9\).
topic-3-1-5.application: After two steps the probabilities are \(5/9\) for \(0\) and \(4/9\) for \(1\). A third step reaches \(0\) by keeping \(0\) or by flipping \(1\): \[P(c_3=0)=\tfrac59\cdot\tfrac23+\tfrac49\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac{10}{27}+\tfrac4{27}=\tfrac{14}{27}.\] The formula gives \(\tfrac12+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac1{27}=14/27\). They agree.
topic-3-1-5.challenge: Write \(p_t=P(c_t=0)\). The run is at \(0\) at time \(t+1\) if it was at \(0\) and kept, or at \(1\) and flipped: \(p_{t+1}=\tfrac23p_t+\tfrac13(1-p_t)=\tfrac13p_t+\tfrac13\). Subtracting \(\tfrac12\) from both sides gives \(p_{t+1}-\tfrac12=\tfrac13\bigl(p_t-\tfrac12\bigr)\). Since \(p_0-\tfrac12=\tfrac12\), induction gives \(p_t-\tfrac12=\tfrac12\left(\tfrac13\right)^t\). As \(t\) grows, \(p_t\) approaches \(\tfrac12\), whatever the start: each step shrinks the difference between the two starting points by a factor of three, so the run gradually forgets where it began.

topic-3-2-1.foundation: By the product rule, it is \(\bra1S\ket1\,\bra1S\ket0\,\bra0S\ket0=(2/3)(1/3)(2/3)=4/27\).
topic-3-2-1.application: A path has weight \(1\) exactly when none of its arrows is \(1\to0\), that is, once the path reaches \(1\) it stays there. From \(0\), the possible paths are \(0\to0\to0\to0\), \(0\to0\to0\to1\), \(0\to0\to1\to1\), and \(0\to1\to1\to1\). The other four contain the arrow \(1\to0\) and have weight \(0\).
topic-3-2-1.challenge: Let \(c_0\) be a fair coin, let \(c_1\) be an independent fair coin, and let \(c_2=c_0\), so the second step copies the starting value. Given \(c_0=0\), the path \(0\to1\to0\) has probability \(1/2\): \(c_1=1\) with probability \(1/2\), and then \(c_2=0\) for certain. But \(P(c_2=0\mid c_1=1)=1/2\), because \(c_1\) says nothing about \(c_0\). The product is \((1/2)(1/2)=1/4\neq1/2\). The second step depends on \(c_0\), not only on the current configuration \(c_1\), so the process is not Markov and the product rule fails.

topic-3-2-2.foundation: The first two steps are free and the third must end at \(1\), so there are \(2\cdot2=4\) paths. The positive count shows that \(1\) is reachable at time \(3\); it says nothing about how likely \(1\) is.
topic-3-2-2.application: From \(0\): \(\bra 0SS\ket 0=\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac23+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac{19}{36}\) and \(\bra 1SS\ket 0=\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac13+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac{17}{36}\). From \(1\): \(\bra 0SS\ket 1=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac23+\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac{17}{48}\) and \(\bra 1SS\ket 1=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac13+\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac34=\tfrac{31}{48}\). Indeed \(\tfrac{19}{36}+\tfrac{17}{36}=1\) and \(\tfrac{17}{48}+\tfrac{31}{48}=1\).
topic-3-2-2.challenge: By the sum and product rules, \[\sum_k\bra kSS\ket i=\sum_k\sum_jP(k\mid j)P(j\mid i)=\sum_jP(j\mid i)\sum_kP(k\mid j).\] The inner sum is \(1\), because the probabilities leaving \(j\) add to \(1\), and the remaining sum \(\sum_jP(j\mid i)\) is \(1\) for the same reason. The two-step weights are nonnegative and add to \(1\) from every start, so two probabilistic steps together form another probabilistic rule.

topic-3-2-3.foundation: COIN sends every distribution to weights \(1/2\) and \(1/2\): \(v^\prime_0=\tfrac12(0.9)+\tfrac12(0.1)=0.5\), and likewise \(v^\prime_1=0.5\). NOT moves each weight along its single arrow, giving \(0.1\) on \(0\) and \(0.9\) on \(1\).
topic-3-2-3.application: We need \(v_0=\tfrac23v_0+\tfrac14v_1\) with \(v_0+v_1=1\). The first equation gives \(\tfrac13v_0=\tfrac14v_1\), so \(v_1=\tfrac43v_0\), and then \(v_0+\tfrac43v_0=1\) gives \(v_0=3/7\) and \(v_1=4/7\). Check: \(v^\prime_0=\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac37+\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac47=\tfrac27+\tfrac17=\tfrac37\).
topic-3-2-3.challenge: Let \(T\) be undone by \(S\). From the definite configuration \(i\), \(T\) produces a distribution \(p_i\), and \(S\) must return it to \(e_i\): \(\sum_jp_i(j)\,S(e_j)=e_i\). Each \(S(e_j)\) is a distribution, and a weighted average of distributions with positive weights equals the definite configuration \(i\) only if every distribution in it is \(e_i\). So \(S(e_j)=e_i\) for every \(j\) with \(p_i(j)\gt 0\). A configuration \(j\) therefore cannot be reached from two different starts \(i\) and \(i^\prime\), since \(S(e_j)\) cannot equal both \(e_i\) and \(e_{i^\prime}\). The \(N\) starts thus reach disjoint, nonempty sets of configurations among only \(N\) configurations, so each set has exactly one element. Each start goes to a single configuration, so \(T\) is deterministic, and different starts go to different configurations, so \(T\) is reversible.

topic-3-3-1.foundation: The product is \((-1/2)(1/3)(-3/4)=1/8\). Two negative factors give a positive contribution.
topic-3-3-1.application: Include the initial weight: \((-2)(1/2)(-1/3)=1/3\). The arrow product alone is \(-1/6\).
topic-3-3-1.challenge: One sign reversal multiplies the product by \(-1\); two multiply it by \((-1)^2=1\), leaving it unchanged. Count occurrences along the path, including repeated uses of an arrow.

topic-3-3-2.foundation: The total is \(1/3-1/2+1/6=0\). All three contributions are nonzero; their sum vanishes by cancellation.
topic-3-3-2.application: The total is \(ca+db=1/4+d/2\). The three cases give \(1/2\), \(1/8\), and \(0\): reinforcement, partial cancellation, and complete cancellation.
topic-3-3-2.challenge: The final weights are \((1/2,-1/2)\). Contributions reinforce at each endpoint. The entries sum to zero, but they belong to different configurations and do not cancel one another.

topic-3-3-3.foundation: The new weights are \(((1-1)/2,(1+1)/2)=(0,1)\). Contributions cancel at \(0\) and reinforce at \(1\).
topic-3-3-3.application: To \(0\), the paths through \(0\) and \(1\) contribute \(1/2\) and \(-1/2\). To \(1\), they contribute \(1/2\) and \((-1/\sqrt2)(-1/\sqrt2)=1/2\). The final weights are \((0,1)\).
topic-3-3-3.challenge: Each endpoint receives \(1/2+1/2=1\), so the final weights are \((1,1)\). Both definite inputs give the same weights \((1,1)/\sqrt2\) after one step; the input cannot be recovered. The missing negative sign removes the cancellation.

topic-3-4-1.foundation: The return weight is \(a^2+b^2\), and the switch weight is \(ab+ba=2ab\). NOT requires these to be \(0\) and \(1\). For real weights, \(a^2+b^2=0\) forces both weights to vanish, making \(2ab=1\) impossible.
topic-3-4-1.application: To \(0\): \[\bra0\sqrt X\ket1\,\bra0\sqrt X\ket0+\bra1\sqrt X\ket1\,\bra0\sqrt X\ket1=\tfrac14\bigl((1-i)(1+i)+(1+i)(1-i)\bigr)=1.\] To \(1\): \[\bra0\sqrt X\ket1\,\bra1\sqrt X\ket0+\bigl(\bra1\sqrt X\ket1\bigr)^2=\tfrac14\bigl((1-i)^2+(1+i)^2\bigr)=0.\] Two steps of \(\sqrt X\) send \(1\) to \(0\), as NOT does.
topic-3-4-1.challenge: Two steps from \(0\) give weight \(a^2+b^2\) at \(0\) and \(2ab\) at \(1\), and from \(1\) the same by symmetry. We need \(a^2+b^2=0\) and \(2ab=1\). If \(a\) and \(b\) were real, the first equation would force \(a=b=0\), contradicting the second. Over the complex numbers, \(a^2=-b^2\) gives \(a=\pm ib\). With \(a=ib\), \(2ib^2=1\), so \(b^2=-i/2\) and \(b=\pm(1-i)/2\), \(a=\pm(1+i)/2\). With \(a=-ib\), \(b^2=i/2\), so \(b=\pm(1+i)/2\) and \(a=\pm(1-i)/2\). There are four solutions: \(S\), \(-S\), and the two operations obtained from them by conjugating every weight. Each is unitary.

topic-3-4-2.foundation: Adding first, \(|1/2+i/2|^2=\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12\). Squaring each path separately also gives \(\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12\). The two contributions point in perpendicular directions in the complex plane, so they neither reinforce nor cancel.
topic-3-4-2.application: Adding first gives \((0.4)^2=0.16\). Squaring first gives \(0.36+0.04=0.40\). Partial destructive interference lowers the probability.
topic-3-4-2.challenge: \(\phi\) and \(-\phi\) have the same cosine, so they give the same probabilities. Before \(H\), multiply the amplitude at configuration \(1\) by \(e^{-i\pi/2}\). This changes the probability to \((1+\sin\phi)/2\), which differs for \(\phi\) and \(-\phi\) unless \(\sin\phi=0\).

topic-3-4-3.foundation: Each final amplitude has magnitude \(1/2\), so each complete configuration has probability \(1/4\). The record is one in \(01\) and \(11\), giving total probability \(1/2\).
topic-3-4-3.application: The input amplitude \(1/\sqrt2\) at \(00\) gives \(+1/2\) at both \(00\) and \(10\). The input amplitude \(1/\sqrt2\) at \(11\) gives \(+1/2\) at \(01\) and \(-1/2\) at \(11\). The contributions to first-label value one have different complete endpoints, \(10\) and \(11\), so their probabilities add rather than their amplitudes.
topic-3-4-3.challenge: After the final H, the amplitudes in order \(00,01,10,11\) are \((1/2,1/2,1/2,-1/2)\). Controlled-NOT exchanges \(10\) and \(11\), giving \((1/2,1/2,-1/2,1/2)\). The probability that the first label is one remains \(1/2\). Only before recombination does this controlled-NOT undo the original recording: after H, the first label has changed, so the same operation no longer clears the record on both contributing alternatives.

topic-4-1-1.foundation: The vector is \(\bigl(1/\sqrt3,\;i\sqrt{2/3}\bigr)^T\). The squared magnitudes are \(1/3\) and \(|i|^2\cdot2/3=2/3\), which add to \(1\).
topic-4-1-1.application: The vector is \((1/\sqrt2,\,0,\,0,\,-1/\sqrt2)^T\). The configurations \(00\) and \(11\) each have probability \(1/2\); \(01\) and \(10\) have probability \(0\).
topic-4-1-1.challenge: Comparing coordinates: \((a+b)/\sqrt2=1\) and \((a-b)/\sqrt2=0\), so \(a=b=1/\sqrt2\). The state \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\) is a superposition of \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\), but in the basis \(\{(\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2,(\ket0-\ket1)/\sqrt2\}\) it is a single basis vector, while \(\ket0\) becomes a superposition. Whether a state is a superposition depends on the basis.

topic-4-1-4.foundation: With \(U_{ji}=\bra jU\ket i\), the matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}\). Its columns give \(U\ket0=i\ket1\) and \(U\ket1=-i\ket0\).
topic-4-1-4.application: \(XH=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(HX=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\). Their first columns give \(XH\ket0=\ket+\) and \(HX\ket0=\ket-\). These states are orthogonal, so they do not differ by a global phase. A measurement in the \(\pm\) basis distinguishes them with certainty.
topic-4-1-4.challenge: The rule sends \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\) to themselves after normalization. A linear map with those actions would be the identity. On \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\), the rule instead gives \((\ket0+2\ket1)/\sqrt5\). It is therefore nonlinear and cannot describe deterministic closed-system evolution.

topic-4-1-5.foundation: \(\operatorname{diag}(1,i)^\dagger=\operatorname{diag}(1,-i)\), and their product is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,(-i)i)=I\), so the first is unitary. For the second, the adjoint is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\), and \(A^\dagger A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&5\end{pmatrix}\neq I\), so it is not.
topic-4-1-5.application: \(U^\dagger=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\\-i&1\end{pmatrix}\). Their product has diagonal entries \((1+(-i)i)/2=1\) and off-diagonal entries \((i-i)/2=0\), so \(U^\dagger U=I\). After the two steps, the amplitude to return to the initial configuration is one, and the amplitude to reach the other configuration is zero.
topic-4-1-5.challenge: For all \(\ket\phi,\ket\psi\): \(\braket\phi{AB\psi}=\braket{A^\dagger\phi}{B\psi}=\braket{B^\dagger A^\dagger\phi}\psi\). This is the defining property of \((AB)^\dagger\), so \((AB)^\dagger=B^\dagger A^\dagger\). For unitaries \(U,V\): \((UV)^\dagger UV=V^\dagger U^\dagger UV=V^\dagger V=I\).

topic-4-2-1.foundation: The squared norm is \(1+|2i|^2=5\), so the state is \((\ket0+2i\ket1)/\sqrt5\). The probabilities are \(1/5\) and \(4/5\).
topic-4-2-1.application: Multiply by the global phase \(-i\): \(-i(i\ket0-\ket1)/\sqrt2=(\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). Now the first coordinate is real and positive, \(\cos\tfrac\theta2=1/\sqrt2\), so \(\theta=\pi/2\), and \(e^{i\phi}=i\), so \(\phi=\pi/2\).
topic-4-2-1.challenge: A sequence of operations is a matrix \(V\), and \(V(e^{i\gamma}\ket\psi)=e^{i\gamma}V\ket\psi\) by linearity. Every coordinate is multiplied by \(e^{i\gamma}\), which has magnitude \(1\), so every probability is unchanged. If \(\ket0-\ket1=e^{i\gamma}(\ket0+\ket1)\), comparing coordinates would give \(e^{i\gamma}=1\) and \(e^{i\gamma}=-1\) at once, which is impossible.

topic-4-2-2.foundation: Outcome \(0\) has probability \(1/5\) and leaves \(\ket0\); outcome \(1\) has probability \(4/5\) and leaves \(\ket1\).
topic-4-2-2.application: The first measurement gives \(0\) with probability \(3/4\) and leaves \(\ket0\), after which the second gives \(0\) for certain. Likewise for \(1\). So \(P(00)=3/4\), \(P(11)=1/4\), and \(P(01)=P(10)=0\).
topic-4-2-2.challenge: \(H\ket0=(\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\), so the first measurement gives \(0\) or \(1\) with probability \(1/2\) each and leaves \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\). Applying \(H\) to either gives an equal superposition, so the second measurement is again \(0\) or \(1\) with probability \(1/2\). All four pairs have probability \(1/4\). Without the middle measurement, \(HH\ket0=\ket0\), and the outcome is \(0\) with certainty. The measurement leaves a definite configuration, and the two paths can no longer interfere.

topic-6-1-1.foundation: Each joint amplitude is a product of local amplitudes, in the order \(00,01,10,11\): the first is \(\bigl(\tfrac1{\sqrt2},0,\tfrac1{\sqrt2},0\bigr)^T\), and the second is \(\bigl(0,\tfrac35,0,\tfrac45\bigr)^T\).
topic-6-1-1.application: \((H\otimes I)\ket{01}=(H\ket0)\otimes\ket1=(\ket{01}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). \((I\otimes H)\ket{01}=\ket0\otimes(H\ket1)=(\ket{00}-\ket{01})/\sqrt2\). The same gate on a different qubit gives a different joint state.
topic-6-1-1.challenge: The coordinates of \(a\otimes b\) are \(a_ib_j\), so \(\braket{a\otimes b}{c\otimes d}=\sum_{i,j}(a_ib_j)^*c_id_j=\Bigl(\sum_ia_i^*c_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_jb_j^*d_j\Bigr)=\braket ac\braket bd\). With \(c=a\) and \(d=b\), \(\|a\otimes b\|^2=\|a\|^2\|b\|^2=1\) for unit vectors.

topic-6-1-2.foundation: Yes: \(\tfrac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}\otimes\tfrac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}=\ket+\ket+\). Every product of the local amplitudes \(1/\sqrt2\) is \(1/2\).
topic-6-1-2.application: The sign depends only on the second label, so the state is \(\tfrac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}\otimes\tfrac{\ket0-\ket1}{\sqrt2}=\ket+\ket-\). The second qubit gives \(0\) with probability \(1/2\).
topic-6-1-2.challenge: For a product \((a\ket0+b\ket1)\otimes(c\ket0+d\ket1)\), \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}=acbd=adbc=\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}\). Conversely, suppose the condition holds. If \(\alpha_{00}\neq0\), then \((\alpha_{00}\ket0+\alpha_{10}\ket1)\otimes(\ket0+\tfrac{\alpha_{01}}{\alpha_{00}}\ket1)\) has amplitudes \(\alpha_{00},\alpha_{01},\alpha_{10}\), and \(\alpha_{10}\alpha_{01}/\alpha_{00}=\alpha_{11}\). If \(\alpha_{00}=0\), the condition gives \(\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}=0\): if \(\alpha_{01}=0\) the state is \(\ket1\otimes(\alpha_{10}\ket0+\alpha_{11}\ket1)\), and if \(\alpha_{10}=0\) it is \((\alpha_{01}\ket0+\alpha_{11}\ket1)\otimes\ket1\).

topic-6-1-3.foundation: \(2^{10}=1024\) amplitudes, but a measurement returns only \(10\) bits.
topic-6-1-3.application: \(2^{40}\cdot16\) bytes \(\approx1.8\times10^{13}\) bytes, about \(18\) terabytes. Each additional qubit doubles this.
topic-6-1-3.challenge: \((U_1\otimes\cdots\otimes U_n)(\ket{\psi_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\ket{\psi_n})=U_1\ket{\psi_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes U_n\ket{\psi_n}\), so it suffices to multiply each \(2\times2\) matrix by its pair of amplitudes: \(n\) small multiplications. The state space has \(2^n\) dimensions, yet this computation is easy to simulate. Difficulty requires entangling operations, not a large state space alone.

topic-6-2-1.foundation: \(H\ket1=(\ket0-\ket1)/\sqrt2\), giving \((\ket{00}-\ket{10})/\sqrt2\). CNOT sends \(10\) to \(11\), so the result is \((\ket{00}-\ket{11})/\sqrt2\), the Bell state \(\ket{\Phi^-}\).
topic-6-2-1.application: From \(\ket{01}\): \((\ket{01}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\to(\ket{01}+\ket{10})/\sqrt2\), the Bell state \(\ket{\Psi^+}\). From \(\ket{11}\): \((\ket{01}-\ket{11})/\sqrt2\to(\ket{01}-\ket{10})/\sqrt2\), the Bell state \(\ket{\Psi^-}\).
topic-6-2-1.challenge: The circuit is unitary, and a unitary preserves inner products, so it maps the orthonormal computational basis to an orthonormal set of four vectors in a four-dimensional space: a basis, the Bell basis. The inverse circuit undoes the gates in reverse order: CNOT, then \(H\) on the first qubit, since each is its own inverse. Followed by a computational-basis measurement, it identifies which Bell state was present.

topic-6-2-2.foundation: A product would need \(ac=ad=bc=1/2\) and \(bd=-1/2\). Then \((ac)(bd)=-1/4\) while \((ad)(bc)=1/4\), but both equal \(abcd\). So no product exists: the state is entangled.
topic-6-2-2.application: The product condition \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}=\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}\) reads \(\varepsilon=0\) (up to the common normalization). Only \(\varepsilon=0\), the state \(\ket{00}\), is a product. However small \(\varepsilon\neq0\) is, the state is entangled, though only slightly.
topic-6-2-2.challenge: After outcome \(0\), the second qubit is proportional to \(\alpha_{00}\ket0+\alpha_{01}\ket1\); after outcome \(1\), to \(\alpha_{10}\ket0+\alpha_{11}\ket1\). These describe the same state exactly when the two vectors are proportional, that is, when \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}=\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}\), which is the product condition. So the conditional state is the same for both outcomes exactly when the state is a product.

topic-6-2-3.application: \(p(00)=p(01)=p(11)=1/3\) and \(p(10)=0\). The first qubit gives \(0\) with probability \(2/3\) and \(1\) with \(1/3\); the second gives \(0\) with \(1/3\) and \(1\) with \(2/3\). Finally, \(p(\text{second}=1\mid\text{first}=0)=p(01)/p(\text{first}=0)=\tfrac{1/3}{2/3}=\tfrac12\).
topic-6-2-3.challenge: The Bell state gives 00 and 11 with probability one half each: the 01 and 10 amplitudes cancel. Each component of the classical mixture gives all four outcomes with probability one quarter, so their probability average does too. The mixture describes separate preparation alternatives, not coherent paths in the same pure state.

topic-6-3-1.foundation: \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\) and \((\ket{01}+\ket{10})/\sqrt2\). In neither case is the result two copies of \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\), which would be \((\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10}+\ket{11})/2\).
topic-6-3-1.application: CNOT gives \(\alpha\ket{00}+\beta\ket{11}\); two copies are \(\alpha^2\ket{00}+\alpha\beta\ket{01}+\alpha\beta\ket{10}+\beta^2\ket{11}\). The \(\ket{01}\) amplitudes require \(\alpha\beta=0\), so the state is \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\), up to a global phase. Only the basis states are copied.
topic-6-3-1.challenge: By linearity, \(U\tfrac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}\ket0=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(U\ket{00}+U\ket{10})=\tfrac{\ket{00}+\ket{11}}{\sqrt2}\). Its amplitudes give \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}=\tfrac12\neq0=\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}\), so it is entangled. Copying basis states forces entangling superpositions; it cannot copy them.

topic-6-3-2.foundation: \(\braket0+=1/\sqrt2\), while \(\braket{00}{++}=\braket0+^2=1/2\). The inputs \(\ket0\ket0\) and \(\ket+\ket0\) have overlap \(1/\sqrt2\), so a unitary would keep that overlap, but the desired outputs \(\ket{00}\) and \(\ket{++}\) have overlap \(1/2\).
topic-6-3-2.application: Take \(U=(H\otimes H)\,\mathrm{CNOT}\,(H\otimes I)\). For \(\ket+\ket0\): \(H\otimes I\) gives \(\ket{00}\), CNOT leaves it, and \(H\otimes H\) gives \(\ket+\ket+\). For \(\ket-\ket0\): \(\ket{10}\to\ket{11}\to\ket-\ket-\). Orthogonal states can be copied; the no-cloning theorem forbids only a cloner for nonorthogonal ones.
topic-6-3-2.challenge: Inner products are preserved: \(\braket\phi\psi=\braket\phi\psi^2\braket{e_\phi}{e_\psi}\). Taking magnitudes with \(c=|\braket\phi\psi|\), we get \(c=c^2|\braket{e_\phi}{e_\psi}|\leq c^2\). So \(c=0\) or \(c\geq1\); since \(c\leq1\) for unit vectors, \(c=0\) or \(c=1\). The states are orthogonal, or equal up to phase. A machine that keeps a record of what it copied gains nothing.

topic-6-3-3.foundation: With probability \(1/2\), Alice obtains \(0\) and Bob’s qubit is \(\ket0\); otherwise it is \(\ket1\). Bob obtains \(0\) with probability \(\tfrac12\cdot1+\tfrac12\cdot0=\tfrac12\), exactly as without Alice’s measurement.
topic-6-3-3.application: \((X\otimes I)\ket{\Phi^+}=(\ket{10}+\ket{01})/\sqrt2\). Bob obtains \(0\) and \(1\) with probability \(1/2\) each, as before. Only the correlations between the two qubits have changed.
topic-6-3-3.challenge: For Alice’s computational-basis choice, Bob’s probability is \(\tfrac12|a|^2+\tfrac12|b|^2=1/2\). For her \(\pm\) choice, it is \(\tfrac14|a+b|^2+\tfrac14|a-b|^2=\tfrac12(|a|^2+|b|^2)=1/2\). The cross terms cancel. Thus changing Bob’s measurement basis cannot reveal Alice’s choice. Matching probabilities in just one basis would not establish this: \(\ket+\) and \(\ket-\), for example, agree in the computational basis but are distinguishable in another.

topic-6-4-1.foundation: Alice holds two qubits, the input and her half of the Bell pair; Bob holds one. The state is \(\ket1\otimes\tfrac{\ket{00}+\ket{11}}{\sqrt2}=\tfrac{\ket{100}+\ket{111}}{\sqrt2}\).
topic-6-4-1.application: CNOT gives \((\ket{110}+\ket{101})/\sqrt2\). \(H\) on the first qubit gives \(\tfrac12\bigl(\ket{010}+\ket{001}-\ket{110}-\ket{101}\bigr)\). Grouped: \(\tfrac12\bigl(\ket{00}\ket1+\ket{01}\ket0-\ket{10}\ket1-\ket{11}\ket0\bigr)\), which matches \(X^nZ^m\ket1\) for each outcome \((m,n)\).
topic-6-4-1.challenge: Bob’s qubit before correction is \(X^nZ^m\ket0=X^n\ket0=\ket n\), and \(Z^m\) does not change a basis state, up to sign. With probability \(1/2\), \(n=1\) and Bob holds \(\ket1\) instead of \(\ket0\). Both classical bits are needed.

topic-6-4-2.application: Bob holds \(XZ\ket+=X\ket-=-\ket-\). He applies \(X\), giving \(-X\ket-=\ket-\), and then \(Z\), giving \(Z\ket-=\ket+\).
topic-6-4-2.challenge: He applies \(X^nZ^m\) to \(X^nZ^m\ket\psi\). If \(m=0\) or \(n=0\), this is \(X^{2n}\ket\psi\) or \(Z^{2m}\ket\psi\), which is \(\ket\psi\). If \(m=n=1\), it is \(XZXZ\ket\psi\); since \(ZX=-XZ\), \(XZXZ=-XXZZ=-I\), giving \(-\ket\psi\), the same state up to a global phase.

topic-6-4-3.foundation: His qubit is \(X^nZ^m\ket0=\pm\ket n\), with \(n=0\) or \(1\) equally likely, so he obtains \(0\) with probability \(1/2\).
topic-6-4-3.application: \(Z^m\) changes only signs, so \(Z^m\ket\psi\) gives \(0\) with probability \(|\alpha|^2\); \(X\) swaps the amplitudes, giving \(|\beta|^2\). Averaging over \(n\), Bob obtains \(0\) with probability \(\tfrac12|\alpha|^2+\tfrac12|\beta|^2=\tfrac12\), independent of \(\psi\).
topic-6-4-3.challenge: The conditional state is \(\ket m\ket n\ket\psi\). Alice’s two qubits are basis states, and each pair \((m,n)\) has probability \(1/4\), independent of \(\psi\). Her remaining registers and the classical record therefore contain no second copy of the unknown input. This describes the systems in this protocol; it does not assert that an external preparer could not already have held another copy.

topic-7-1-1.foundation: \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\) are constant; \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\) are balanced.
topic-7-1-1.application: There are \(2^4=16\) functions. Two are constant. A balanced function outputs \(1\) on exactly two of the four inputs, chosen in \(\binom42=6\) ways. The remaining \(16-2-6=8\) are neither, which is why the promise is needed.
topic-7-1-1.challenge: If two queried values differ, \(f\) is balanced. If \(2^{n-1}+1\) queried values all agree, \(f\) cannot be balanced, since a balanced function takes each value on only \(2^{n-1}\) inputs; so \(f\) is constant. With only \(2^{n-1}\) queries all returning \(0\), \(f\) could be the constant \(0\) or the balanced function that is \(1\) on all the unqueried inputs, so the algorithm cannot be sure.

topic-7-1-2.foundation: \((0,1)\), which is balanced, and \((1,1)\), which is constant. One reply is consistent with both answers.
topic-7-1-2.application: If \(f(00)=f(01)\), query \(f(10)\). If it differs, answer “balanced”; if it agrees, three of the four values agree, which rules out a balanced function, so answer “constant.” The worst case uses three queries, matching \(2^{n-1}+1\) for \(n=2\).
topic-7-1-2.challenge: Average the success probability over the four functions, each weighted \(1/4\). Whatever input \(x\) is queried and whatever value \(v\) is returned, exactly two functions are consistent with the reply, one constant and one balanced, and they are equally weighted. So any answer is right for exactly one of them, and the average success is \(1/2\). Some function must therefore have success probability at most \(1/2\).

topic-7-1-3.foundation: \(\ket{00}\to\ket{01}\), \(\ket{01}\to\ket{00}\), \(\ket{10}\to\ket{10}\), and \(\ket{11}\to\ket{11}\): the target flips when the input is \(0\).
topic-7-1-3.application: \(U_f\) fixes \(\ket{00}\) and \(\ket{01}\) and exchanges \(\ket{10}\) and \(\ket{11}\): the matrix of CNOT. It is a permutation matrix, whose columns are distinct basis vectors and hence orthonormal, so \(U_f^\dagger U_f=I\).
topic-7-1-3.challenge: Overwriting sends \(\ket{x,0}\) and \(\ket{x,1}\) to the same state \(\ket{x,f(x)}\), so it is not one-to-one, and a unitary is invertible. For constant \(f\), \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\) both go to \(\ket{f(0)}\), again merging two orthogonal states. Keeping the input and adding into the target avoids both problems.

topic-7-2-1.foundation: Both inputs flip the target: \((\ket{01}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2=\ket+\ket1\), a product state.
topic-7-2-1.application: \((0,0)\): \(\ket+\ket0\). \((1,1)\): \(\ket+\ket1\). \((0,1)\): \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). \((1,0)\): \((\ket{01}+\ket{10})/\sqrt2\). The constant functions give product states; the balanced ones give entangled states.
topic-7-2-1.challenge: Each run reveals one input chosen uniformly from \(N=2^n\). After \(k\) distinct inputs have been seen, a new one appears with probability \((N-k)/N\), taking \(N/(N-k)\) runs on average. Summing, \(N\bigl(1+\tfrac12+\dots+\tfrac1N\bigr)\approx N\ln N\) runs are needed, more than the \(N\) queries of a classical algorithm that simply asks each input once.

topic-7-2-2.foundation: \(00\) and \(11\), each with probability \(1/2\). One run reveals one pair \((x,f(x))\), a single function value.
topic-7-2-2.application: The first run shows one input. Each later run shows the other input with probability \(1/2\), taking \(2\) runs on average. The total is \(1+2=3\) runs on average, worse than the two classical queries.
topic-7-2-2.challenge: The probability of input \(x\) is the total squared amplitude of the configurations beginning with \(x\). There is exactly one, \(\ket{x,f(x)}\), with amplitude \(1/\sqrt2\), whatever \(f\) is. The input register alone reveals nothing about \(f\).

topic-7-2-3.foundation: \(H\) on the first qubit gives \(\tfrac12(\ket{00}+\ket{10}+\ket{01}-\ket{11})\). The input is \(0\) with probability \(\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12\), and \(1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\). The target record prevents any cancellation.
topic-7-2-3.application: \(U_f\) leaves \(\ket+\ket0\) unchanged, and \(H\) turns it into \(\ket0\ket0\). The input is \(0\) with certainty: here the target holds no record, because it is the same in both branches.
topic-7-2-3.challenge: Run \(U_f\) on \(\ket+\ket0\), apply \(H\) to the input, and measure it. Constant functions always give \(0\); balanced ones give \(0\) or \(1\) with probability \(1/2\) each. Answer “balanced” on outcome \(1\), and “not sure” on \(0\). The answer “balanced” is never wrong, but it is given for a balanced function only half the time. Deutsch’s algorithm, whose target leaves no record, succeeds every time.

topic-7-3-1.foundation: \(X(\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2=(i\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2=i(\ket0-i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). This is not a multiple of \((\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\), so it is not an eigenvector.
topic-7-3-1.application: \(X(a,b)^T=(b,a)^T\), so \(b=\lambda a\) and \(a=\lambda b\), giving \(\lambda^2=1\). For \(\lambda=1\), \(a=b\): the state \(\ket+\). For \(\lambda=-1\), \(b=-a\): the state \(\ket-\). Up to global phase, these are the only two.
topic-7-3-1.challenge: \(X(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^T=(\sin\theta,\cos\theta)^T\), whose overlap with the original is \(2\cos\theta\sin\theta=\sin2\theta\). The target keeps no record when the flipped state equals the original up to a factor, which requires an overlap of magnitude \(1\): \(\sin2\theta=\pm1\), so \(\theta=\pm\pi/4\) up to multiples of \(\pi\). These are \(\ket+\) and \(\ket-\), up to sign. For any other target, the flip leaves a partial record that reduces the interference.

topic-7-3-2.foundation: The signs are \((-1)^{f(0)}=-1\) and \((-1)^{f(1)}=+1\), so the result is \(\tfrac{-\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}\otimes\ket-=-\ket-\ket-\).
topic-7-3-2.application: Since \(X\ket+=\ket+\), either value of \(f(x)\) leaves the target unchanged with eigenvalue \(+1\). For all four functions the output is \(\ket+\ket+\). The target is unentangled, but no information about \(f\) reaches the input. The \(\ket-\) preparation matters because a flip has eigenvalue \(-1\), giving different phases to different function values.
topic-7-3-2.challenge: For each basis input, \(U_f\ket x\ket-=(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\ket-\), because a flip multiplies \(\ket-\) by \(-1\) and no flip leaves it alone. By linearity, the superposition becomes \(\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\ket-\), up to the factor \(2^{-n/2}\). The target factors out as \(\ket-\), so it carries no record of \(x\).

topic-7-3-3.foundation: \(\ket{00}\) passes unchanged, with \(Z\) acting on \(0\): the result is \(\ket{00}\). For \(\ket{10}\): CNOT gives \(\ket{11}\), \(Z\) gives \(-\ket{11}\), and CNOT gives \(-\ket{10}\). The phases are \((-1)^x\), and the answer bit is back to \(0\).
topic-7-3-3.application: On \(\ket{x,y}\): CNOT gives \(\ket{x,y\oplus x}\), \(Z\) multiplies by \((-1)^{x\oplus y}\), and CNOT restores \(\ket{x,y}\). The operation is \(\ket{x,y}\mapsto(-1)^{x\oplus y}\ket{x,y}\), that is, \(Z\otimes Z\). Only when \(y=0\) is the phase \((-1)^{f(x)}\); a workspace starting elsewhere adds an unwanted phase.
topic-7-3-3.challenge: CNOT gives \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\), and \(Z\) gives \((\ket{00}-\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). \(H\) on the input gives \(\tfrac12(\ket{00}+\ket{10}-\ket{01}+\ket{11})\), so the input is \(0\) or \(1\) with probability \(1/2\) each. With uncomputation, the state before \(H\) is \((\ket0-\ket1)\ket0/\sqrt2=\ket-\ket0\), and \(H\) gives \(\ket1\ket0\): outcome \(1\) with certainty. The answer bit left behind is a record that blocks the interference.

topic-7-4-1.application: \((0,0)\): \(s=(1,1)\), amplitudes \((1,0)\). \((1,1)\): \(s=(-1,-1)\), amplitudes \((-1,0)\). \((0,1)\): \(s=(1,-1)\), amplitudes \((0,1)\). \((1,0)\): \(s=(-1,1)\), amplitudes \((0,-1)\). The constant functions give \(0\) and the balanced ones give \(1\), each up to sign.
topic-7-4-1.challenge: Before the final step the input is \((s_0\ket0+s_1\ket1)/\sqrt2\) with \(s_x=\pm1\), so each outcome has probability \(1/2\). \(X\) only swaps the two amplitudes, leaving both probabilities at \(1/2\). Only an operation that combines the two amplitudes, such as \(H\), turns the relative sign into a definite outcome.

topic-7-4-2.foundation: One query to \(U_f\). Besides it: one \(X\) to prepare \(\ket1\), two \(H\) gates to prepare \(\ket+\ket-\), one final \(H\), and one measurement.
topic-7-4-2.challenge: \(H\) on each qubit sends every \(\ket x\) to a superposition in which \(\ket{0^n}\) has amplitude \(2^{-n/2}\). Applied to \(2^{-n/2}\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\), it gives \(\ket{0^n}\) the amplitude \(2^{-n}\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\). For constant \(f\), this is \(\pm1\), so the outcome is \(0^n\) with certainty; for balanced \(f\), the signs cancel exactly and the outcome is never \(0^n\). One query suffices, against \(2^{n-1}+1\) classically.

topic-7-4-3.foundation: Prepare: \(X\) and two \(H\) gates make \(\ket+\ket-\). Encode: one query to \(U_f\) puts \(f\) into relative phase. Recombine: \(H\) on the input. Measure: the input in the computational basis.
topic-7-4-3.application: \(X\ket+=\ket+\), so \(U_f\) leaves \(\ket+\ket+\) unchanged, and the final \(H\) gives \(\ket0\). The algorithm reports “constant” for a balanced function: with the wrong target, the function leaves no mark at all.
topic-7-4-3.challenge: \(U_f\ket0\ket-=(-1)^{f(0)}\ket0\ket-\), which depends only on \(f(0)\), and only through a global sign. The final \(H\) gives \(\pm\ket+\), so each outcome has probability \(1/2\). Without a superposition of inputs, the query sees only one input, and no relative phase forms.

topic-9-1-1.foundation: The marked labels are \(011\), \(101\), and \(110\): three of the eight. A random label is marked with probability \(3/8\).
topic-9-1-1.application: The marked label is equally likely to be in any of the \(8\) positions of the order, so the expected number of queries is \((1+2+\dots+8)/8=(N+1)/2=4.5\).
topic-9-1-1.challenge: Consider first a deterministic algorithm. Until it finds the label, every answer is \(0\), so its sequence of queries before success is fixed in advance: some \(k\) labels. It succeeds exactly when the marked label is among them, with probability at most \(k/N\). A randomized algorithm is an average of deterministic ones, so it too succeeds with probability at most \(k/N\). Constant success therefore needs a number of queries proportional to \(N\).

topic-9-1-2.application: Every amplitude is \(1/\sqrt8\), except the marked one, which is \(-1/\sqrt8\). The marked label is measured with probability \(1/8\), the same as before marking.
topic-9-1-2.challenge: \(O_f\) multiplies each amplitude by \(\pm1\), so it leaves every magnitude unchanged. Moreover \(O_f^2=I\), so any number of applications equals \(I\) or \(O_f\). The probabilities never change; an operation that mixes amplitudes is needed.

topic-9-1-3.foundation: The mean is \(\tfrac14\). The entries \(\tfrac12\) become \(2\cdot\tfrac14-\tfrac12=0\), and \(-\tfrac12\) becomes \(\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1\). The result is \((0,1,0,0)\): the marked label \(01\) with certainty.
topic-9-1-3.application: Write \(a=1/\sqrt8\). After marking, seven amplitudes are \(a\) and one is \(-a\), so the mean is \(6a/8=3a/4\). The unmarked amplitudes become \(3a/2-a=a/2\), and the marked one becomes \(3a/2+a=5a/2\). The success probability is \((5a/2)^2=25/32\approx0.78\), up from \(1/8\). The seven unmarked probabilities, \(1/32\) each, account for the remaining \(7/32\).

topic-9-2-1.foundation: \(\ket G=(\ket{011}+\ket{101})/\sqrt2\), and \(\ket B\) is the equal superposition of the other six labels, each with amplitude \(1/\sqrt6\).
topic-9-2-1.challenge: \(O_f\ket G=-\ket G\) and \(O_f\ket B=\ket B\). With \(\ket s=\sin\theta\ket G+\cos\theta\ket B\), we have \(\braket sG=\sin\theta\) and \(\braket sB=\cos\theta\), so \(D\ket G=2\sin\theta\ket s-\ket G\) and \(D\ket B=2\cos\theta\ket s-\ket B\). Both are combinations of \(\ket G\) and \(\ket B\), so the state never leaves their plane.

topic-9-2-2.application: \(\theta=30^\circ\), as for \(N=4\), \(M=1\). One iteration turns the state to \(3\theta=90^\circ\), the good direction, so one iteration succeeds with certainty.
topic-9-2-2.challenge: After one iteration the success probability is \(\sin^2(3\theta)\), which equals \(1\) when \(3\theta=\pi/2+j\pi\). For \(0\lt\theta\lt\pi/2\) this gives \(\theta=\pi/6\) only, since the next solution, \(\theta=\pi/2\), would mean \(M=N\). And \(\sin^2(\pi/6)=1/4=M/N\).

topic-9-2-3.application: The angle after \(k\) iterations is \((2k+1)\theta\), with \(\theta\approx14.48^\circ\): about \(43.4^\circ\), \(72.4^\circ\), \(101.3^\circ\), and \(130.3^\circ\). The success probabilities \(\sin^2\) of these angles are about \(0.47\), \(0.91\), \(0.96\), and \(0.58\). The best is three iterations; the fourth overshoots.
topic-9-2-3.challenge: The first reflection, across \(\alpha=0\), is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\). The second, across \(\alpha=\theta\), multiplies it on the left: \(\begin{pmatrix}\cos2\theta&\sin2\theta\\\sin2\theta&-\cos2\theta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos2\theta&-\sin2\theta\\\sin2\theta&\cos2\theta\end{pmatrix}\), the rotation by \(2\theta\).

topic-9-3-1.application: \(\sin\theta=1/8\), so \(\theta\approx7.18^\circ\), and \(\pi/(4\theta)-1/2\approx5.8\). Comparing neighbours: \(k=5\) gives \(\sin^2(79^\circ)\approx0.96\), and \(k=6\) gives \(\sin^2(93.4^\circ)\approx0.997\). The best is \(k=6\), with success probability about \(0.997\).
topic-9-3-1.challenge: The state is always \(\sin\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr)\ket G+\cos\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr)\ket B\), and \(\ket G\) gives every marked label the same amplitude \(1/\sqrt M\). So all marked labels have equal probability \(\sin^2\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr)/M\), and given success each has probability \(1/M\). The same argument with \(\ket B\) applies to failure.

topic-9-3-2.foundation: \(\theta=30^\circ\), so the angle is \(7\theta=210^\circ\), and \(\sin^2210^\circ=1/4\): no better than guessing.
topic-9-3-2.application: With \(M=4\), \(\sin\theta=\sqrt{4/16}=1/2\), so \(\theta=\pi/6\). Three iterations give \(\sin^2(7\pi/6)=1/4\). One iteration gives \(\sin^2(3\pi/6)=1\). More marked items do not guarantee better performance with a fixed iteration count: they change the rotation angle, so the stopping time must change too.
topic-9-3-2.challenge: \(p_k=\sin^2\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr)\), and \(\sin^2\) repeats when its argument changes by \(\pi\). Each iteration adds \(2\theta\), so \(p_{k+j}=p_k\) whenever \(2j\theta\) is a multiple of \(\pi\). For \(\theta=\pi/6\), \(2j\theta=j\pi/3\), first a multiple of \(\pi\) at \(j=3\). The sequence is \(\tfrac14,1,\tfrac14,\tfrac14,1,\tfrac14,\dots\), with period \(3\).

topic-9-3-3.foundation: The attempts are independent, so the number needed is geometric with mean \(1/p\). Because each candidate is checked, the algorithm never reports a wrong label.
topic-9-3-3.application: For \(M=4\), \(\sin\theta=\sqrt{4/1024}=1/16\), and \(51\theta\approx51\times3.58^\circ\approx182.7^\circ\), so the success probability is \(\sin^2(182.7^\circ)\approx0.002\). Tuned for \(M=1\) it would be about \(0.999\). Guessing \(M\) wrong can make the search almost certain to fail.
topic-9-3-3.challenge: Each attempt fails with probability at most \(3/4\), and independent failures multiply, so all \(t\) fail with probability at most \((3/4)^t\). We need \(t\ln(3/4)\lt\ln10^{-6}\), that is, \(t\gt\ln10^{-6}/\ln(3/4)\approx48.0\), so \(t=49\).

topic-9-4-1.foundation: \(\sin\theta=\sqrt p=1/3\), so \(\theta\approx19.5^\circ\). The amplitudes are \(\sqrt p=1/3\) and \(\sqrt{1-p}=2\sqrt2/3\).
topic-9-4-1.application: The angle after \(k\) iterations is \((2k+1)\theta\): about \(58.4^\circ\) for \(k=1\) and \(97.4^\circ\) for \(k=2\). The success probabilities are about \(0.73\) and \(0.98\), so \(k=2\) is best.
topic-9-4-1.challenge: \(p=1/4\), so \(\theta=30^\circ\), and one iteration turns the state to \(90^\circ\), the good direction. Directly: \(I-2P_G=Z\) gives \(\ket v=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\ket0-\tfrac12\ket1\). Then \(R_\psi\ket v=2\ket\psi\braket\psi v-\ket v\) with \(\braket\psi v=\tfrac34-\tfrac14=\tfrac12\), giving \(\ket\psi-\ket v=\ket1\).

topic-9-4-2.application: \(A\ket0\bra0A^\dagger=(A\ket0)(A\ket0)^\dagger=\ket\psi\bra\psi\), and \(AIA^\dagger=AA^\dagger=I\), so the product is \(2\ket\psi\bra\psi-I\). It is a product of three unitaries, since \(2\ket0\bra0-I=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,\dots,-1)\) is unitary, and so it is unitary.
topic-9-4-2.challenge: Measuring the prepared state \(\sqrt p\ket G+\sqrt{1-p}\ket B\) gives success with probability \(p\) and leaves a single outcome. Repeating preparation and measurement just gives independent trials, each with success \(p\). The reflection instead rotates the whole state toward \(\ket G\); measurement destroys the superposition that the rotation acts on.

topic-9-4-3.foundation: Trials: about \(1/p=100\). Amplification: about \(\tfrac\pi4/\sqrt p\approx8\) iterations, each using \(A\), \(A^\dagger\), and the success test.
topic-9-4-3.application: Trials: \(10^4\times120=1.2\times10^6\) gates. Amplification: \(\tfrac\pi4\times100\approx79\) iterations of \(100+100+20=220\) gates, about \(1.7\times10^4\) gates, roughly \(70\) times fewer.
topic-9-4-3.challenge: Amplification needs about \(\sqrt N\) iterations, and each uses the preparation, costing about \(N\), so the total is about \(N\sqrt N\). A classical scan of the list costs about \(N\). If the data must be loaded this way, amplification is slower: the advantage depends on the preparation being cheap.

topic-8-1-1.foundation: \(H\): \((\ket{00}+\ket{10})/\sqrt2\). \(X\) on qubit 2: \((\ket{01}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). CNOT flips qubit 2 where qubit 1 is \(1\): \((\ket{01}+\ket{10})/\sqrt2\).
topic-8-1-1.application: \(H\) then CNOT gives \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). CNOT then \(H\) gives \((\ket{00}+\ket{10})/\sqrt2\), because CNOT leaves \(\ket{00}\) unchanged. They do not commute; the two gates share qubit 1.
topic-8-1-1.challenge: On a product state \(\ket a\ket b\), both orders give \(U\ket a\otimes V\ket b\), which is also \((U\otimes V)\ket a\ket b\). The three matrices agree on every product basis state, and every state is a combination of these, so by linearity they are equal.

topic-8-1-2.foundation: One iteration has one oracle use, the first controlled-\(Z\), and four Hadamard gates in the reflection, two before and two after the reflection about \(\ket{00}\). Two more Hadamard gates prepare \(\ket s\) from \(\ket{00}\).
topic-8-1-2.application: \(X\) on qubit 2; \(H\) on qubit 1 and \(H\) on qubit 2, which can act at the same time; \(U_f\) on qubits 1 and 2; \(H\) on qubit 1; measurement of qubit 1.
topic-8-1-2.challenge: Up to \(n\) \(X\) gates before and \(n\) after, on the positions where the string has \(0\). The phase flip computes the AND of \(n-1\) qubits into the workspace with \(n-2\) Toffoli gates, applies a controlled-\(Z\) between the last workspace qubit and the remaining qubit, and uncomputes with \(n-2\) more Toffoli gates. Altogether about \(2n\) \(X\) gates, \(2(n-2)\) Toffoli gates, and one controlled-\(Z\): one box hides a number of gates proportional to \(n\).

topic-8-1-3.foundation: \(b=0\): the identity \(I\). \(b=1\): \(X\). The bit is known when the gate is chosen, so this is a classical choice, not a quantum gate.
topic-8-1-3.application: (a) CNOT gives \(\alpha\ket{00}+\beta\ket{11}\). Measuring the control gives \(0\) with probability \(|\alpha|^2\), leaving \(\ket{00}\), and \(1\) with probability \(|\beta|^2\), leaving \(\ket{11}\). (b) Measuring first gives the same probabilities, leaving \(\ket{00}\) or \(\ket{10}\), and the classical \(X\) turns \(\ket{10}\) into \(\ket{11}\). The results agree: a measurement of the control may be moved past a gate that it controls.
topic-8-1-3.challenge: CNOT gives \(\ket-\ket-\), by phase kickback; \(H\) on the control gives \(\ket1\), so the result is \(1\) with certainty. Measuring first leaves the control in \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\), with the target still \(\ket-\), up to sign; \(H\) then gives \(0\) or \(1\) with probability \(1/2\). A classically controlled gate is not a substitute for a coherent one when the control’s phase matters.

topic-8-2-1.foundation: \(R_P(\pi)=\cos\tfrac\pi2I-i\sin\tfrac\pi2P=-iP\). So \(R_X(\pi)=-iX\) and \(R_Z(\pi)=-iZ\): the Pauli gates, up to the global phase \(-i\).
topic-8-2-1.application: \(HZ=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), and multiplying by \(H\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=X\). Similarly, \(HXH=Z\). For the phase gates, \(S^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i^2)=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)=Z\) and \(T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/2})=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)=S\).
topic-8-2-1.challenge: \(\cos\tfrac\theta2I-i\sin\tfrac\theta2Z=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\cos\tfrac\theta2-i\sin\tfrac\theta2,\;\cos\tfrac\theta2+i\sin\tfrac\theta2\bigr)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\theta/2},e^{i\theta/2})\). Factoring out \(e^{-i\theta/2}\) leaves \(\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\theta})\). So \(S\) is \(R_Z(\pi/2)\) and \(T\) is \(R_Z(\pi/4)\), each up to a global phase.

topic-8-2-2.foundation: It fixes \(\ket{00}\), \(\ket{01}\), and \(\ket{10}\), and sends \(\ket{11}\) to \(-\ket{11}\): the matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,-1)\). The sign appears exactly when both qubits are \(1\), a condition symmetric in the two qubits.
topic-8-2-2.application: \(\ket{10}\to\ket1\ket+\to\ket1X\ket+=\ket1\ket+\to\ket{10}\). \(\ket{11}\to\ket1\ket-\to\ket1X\ket-=-\ket1\ket-\to-\ket{11}\). Only \(\ket{11}\) gains the sign, as for controlled-\(Z\).
topic-8-2-2.challenge: Controlled-\(U\) leaves \(\ket0\ket v\) unchanged and sends \(\ket1\ket v\) to \(\ket1U\ket v=e^{i\phi}\ket1\ket v\). By linearity, \(\ket+\ket v\) becomes \(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\ket0+e^{i\phi}\ket1)\otimes\ket v\), a product state. The eigenvalue moves onto the control as a relative phase; phase kickback in Deutsch’s algorithm is the case \(U=X\), \(\ket v=\ket-\), \(\phi=\pi\).

topic-8-2-3.foundation: \(X\) on qubit 1, controlled-\(Z\), then \(X\) on qubit 1. The first \(X\) turns \(\ket{01}\) into \(\ket{11}\), controlled-\(Z\) gives it the sign, and the second \(X\) restores the label. Every other basis state avoids \(\ket{11}\) and is unchanged.
topic-8-2-3.application: Left side: \((H\otimes H)\ket{00}=\ket s\); the reflection gives \(2\ket{00}\braket{00}s-\ket s=\ket{00}-\ket s\), since \(\braket{00}s=\tfrac12\); and \(H\otimes H\) gives \(\ket s-\ket{00}\). Right side: \(2\ket s\braket s{00}-\ket{00}=\ket s-\ket{00}\). They agree.
topic-8-2-3.challenge: Conjugating by \(X\otimes X\) moves the sign of controlled-\(Z\) from \(\ket{11}\) to \(\ket{00}\), giving \(\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)=-\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)=-(2\ket{00}\bra{00}-I)\). In a Grover iteration the factor \(-1\) is a global phase and changes no probability. If the iteration were controlled by another qubit, the sign would apply only in the branch where the control is \(1\), becoming a relative phase that affects later interference.

topic-8-3-1.foundation: \((H\otimes H)\ket{00}=\ket+\ket+=(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10}+\ket{11})/2\), a product of the two local states.
topic-8-3-1.application: The two \(H\) gates cancel on qubit 1, and \(X\) acts on qubit 2, so the result is \(\ket{01}\). Every gate acts on one qubit, so the circuit is \((HH)\otimes X\), which maps product states to product states.
topic-8-3-1.challenge: Suppose \((A\otimes B)\ket\Phi=\ket u\otimes\ket v\) for unitaries \(A,B\). Applying \(A^\dagger\otimes B^\dagger\) gives \(\ket\Phi=A^\dagger\ket u\otimes B^\dagger\ket v\), a product state, contradicting the assumption that \(\ket\Phi\) is entangled. Local operations can neither create nor remove entanglement.

topic-8-3-2.foundation: Only \(\{H,\text{CNOT}\}\). The first set has only one-qubit gates, which keep product states. The third has only permutations of basis states, which never create a superposition.
topic-8-3-2.application: Each gate sends every basis state to a basis state and is one-to-one, so its matrix is a permutation matrix. A product of permutation matrices is a permutation matrix, so the whole circuit permutes the basis states, and from \(\ket{00}\) it reaches only another basis state.
topic-8-3-2.challenge: Each gate is one of three types placed on at most \(m^3\) choices of wires, so there are at most \(3m^3\) choices per gate and \((3m^3)^g\) circuits of \(g\) gates. There are \(2^{2^n}\) Boolean functions of \(n\) bits, and a circuit computes one function on a chosen output wire, so computing all of them needs \((3m^3)^g\geq2^{2^n}\), that is, \(g\geq2^n/\log_2(3m^3)\). For \(n=20\) and \(m=30\), this is about \(64{,}000\) gates. Universality guarantees that every function can be built, not that it can be built cheaply.

topic-8-3-3.foundation: Errors add at most, so the bound is \(1000\times10^{-6}=10^{-3}\).
topic-8-3-3.challenge: Write \(U_2U_1-V_2V_1=U_2(U_1-V_1)+(U_2-V_2)V_1\). For every unit vector \(v\), \(\|U_2(U_1-V_1)v\|=\|(U_1-V_1)v\|\leq\|U_1-V_1\|\), since \(U_2\) preserves length, and \(\|(U_2-V_2)V_1v\|\leq\|U_2-V_2\|\), since \(V_1v\) is a unit vector. The triangle inequality gives the result; repeating the argument covers \(L\) gates.

topic-8-4-1.foundation: Gate count \(5\). Depth \(3\): the three \(H\) gates form one layer, and the two CNOT gates must follow one another, since both use qubit 2. Width \(3\).
topic-8-4-1.application: Computing uses \(n-1=7\) Toffoli gates (six into workspace bits, one into the output), and uncomputing uses \(6\) more: \(13\) gates. Each gate needs the previous result, so the depth is also \(13\). Width: \(8\) inputs, \(6\) workspace bits, and \(1\) output, \(15\) qubits.
topic-8-4-1.challenge: The tree uses \(4\) Toffoli gates on the input pairs, \(2\) on their results, and \(1\) into the output: \(7\) gates in \(3\) layers. Uncomputing the \(6\) workspace bits takes \(6\) gates in \(2\) layers. Total: \(13\) gates, depth \(5\), and \(6\) workspace bits. The chain has the same gate count and workspace but depth \(13\). For \(n\) bits, the tree’s depth grows like \(2\log_2n\) rather than \(2n\).

topic-8-4-2.foundation: Two: swap qubits 1 and 2, so that qubit 1’s state sits next to qubit 3; apply the CNOT; then swap back.
topic-8-4-2.application: For three qubits: \(2\times3+1=7\) CNOT gates instead of \(1\). For \(n\) qubits, moving one end next to the other takes \(n-2\) SWAP gates, and moving back takes \(n-2\) more: \(6(n-2)+1=6n-11\) CNOT gates.
topic-8-4-2.challenge: Loading costs about \(N\), more than the \(\sqrt N\) search, so a single search costs about \(N\), no better than scanning the data classically. The speedup survives only if the state is cheap to prepare, for example because it is produced by a short computation rather than loaded from data, or because one loaded state is used for many searches.

topic-8-4-3.application: We need \((1-q)^{10^9}\geq0.9\). Since \((1-q)^N\approx e^{-qN}\), this requires \(q\lesssim-\ln0.9/10^9\approx1.05\times10^{-10}\), far below what physical gates achieve. Long computations need error correction.
topic-8-4-3.challenge: Decoding fails after two or three flips: \(3q^2(1-q)+q^3=3q^2-2q^3\). This is smaller than \(q\) exactly for \(0<q<1/2\). But a phase flip gives \(\alpha\ket{000}-\beta\ket{111}\), which generally changes the encoded quantum state without changing any computational-basis bit pattern. Majority voting sees no error. Protecting quantum information therefore requires protection of relative phase as well as of bit values.

topic-10-1-1.foundation: \(2^{29}\lt10^9\lt2^{30}\), so \(N\) has \(30\) bits. With \(n\) bits, \(\sqrt N\approx2^{n/2}\), which is exponential in \(n\), not polynomial.
topic-10-1-1.application: Worst case: \(2^n\). Average: \(\tfrac12\cdot5+\tfrac12\cdot2^n=(5+2^n)/2\), still exponential. A good average needs most inputs, weighted by their probability, to be cheap.
topic-10-1-1.challenge: In the worst case, when \(N\) is prime or a product of two close primes, it tests about \(\sqrt N=2^{n/2}\) divisors. That is exponential in \(n\): trial division is not polynomial-time, although its cost is polynomial in the value \(N\).

topic-10-1-2.foundation: Yes: \(100n\leq100n^2\) for \(n\geq1\), so \(C=100\) works. No: \(n^2\leq C\cdot100n\) fails as soon as \(n\gt 100C\), whatever \(C\) is.
topic-10-1-2.application: At \(n=100\), the costs are \(100{,}000\) and \(10{,}000\), so the quadratic algorithm wins. At \(n=1000\), both cost \(10^6\). At \(n=10{,}000\), the costs are \(10^7\) and \(10^8\), so the linear algorithm wins. Linear growth is eventually better, but the constant moves the crossover to \(1000\). A scaling claim needs the input size and actual costs before it becomes a practical recommendation.
topic-10-1-2.challenge: Comparing the two, \(n^{10}\gt 2^n\) for every \(n\) from \(2\) to \(58\), and \(n^{10}\lt2^n\) from \(n=59\) on. The polynomial algorithm wins only for inputs of at least \(59\) bits, where both costs exceed \(10^{17}\). Asymptotic statements describe eventual growth; at practical sizes, constants and exponents can decide the comparison.

topic-10-1-3.foundation: \((\pi/4)\times1000\approx785\) iterations of \(1050\) gates each: about \(8.2\times10^5\) gates.
topic-10-1-3.application: We need \(785c\lt10^6\), so \(c\lt1273\) gates per query. A more expensive oracle erases the quadratic advantage at this size.
topic-10-1-3.challenge: A costs \(n^{2+k}+n^3\), and B costs \(n^{1+k}+n^4\). For \(k\lt2\), A grows like \(n^3\) and B like \(n^4\): A wins. For \(k=2\), both grow like \(n^4\). For \(k\gt 2\), A grows like \(n^{2+k}\) and B like \(n^{1+k}\): B wins. Fewer queries help only when queries dominate the cost.

topic-10-2-1.foundation: (a) and (c): their answers are yes or no. (b) asks for a number; it can be turned into decision problems, such as “does \(N\) have a factor below \(k\)?”
topic-10-2-1.application: \(d=7\): it satisfies \(1\lt7\lt10\), and \(91=7\times13\). Checking a proposed \(d\) means comparing it with \(1\) and \(k\) and dividing \(N\) by \(d\), which takes time polynomial in the number of digits. The problem is in NP.
topic-10-2-1.challenge: Let the reduction run in time \(p(n)\) on inputs of length \(n\); its output then has length at most \(p(n)\). Solving that instance of \(B\) takes time \(q(p(n))\) for the polynomial \(q\) bounding \(B\)’s algorithm. The total, \(p(n)+q(p(n))\), is a polynomial in \(n\), so \(A\) is in P. If the reduction were slow, or produced an exponentially long instance, the composition would not be polynomial.

topic-10-2-2.foundation: The majority is wrong when at least two runs are wrong: \(3\cdot(1/3)^2\cdot(2/3)+(1/3)^3=6/27+1/27=7/27\approx0.26\), less than \(1/3\).
topic-10-2-2.application: Summing the probability that at least half the runs are wrong, an odd number \(k\) of runs gives error below \(0.01\) first at \(k=47\), where it is about \(0.009\). The error falls exponentially in \(k\), so this kind of repetition is cheap.
topic-10-2-2.challenge: Each run is right with probability \(1/2\), whatever the input. With \(k\) independent fair coins, the majority is a fair coin by symmetry, so its error is still \(1/2\). Majority voting helps only when each run is right with probability bounded above \(1/2\); the gap, here at least \(1/3\) versus \(2/3\), is what repetition amplifies.

topic-10-2-3.application: \(2048^3\approx8.6\times10^9\), against about \(10^{308}\). The polynomial is astronomically smaller, which is why factoring is the standard example of a possible exponential quantum advantage.
topic-10-2-3.challenge: \(\ln N=2048\ln2\approx1420\), so \((\ln N)^{1/3}\approx11.2\) and \((\ln\ln N)^{2/3}\approx3.75\). The exponent is about \(81\), giving \(e^{81}\approx10^{35}\) steps: far better than trial division, still far worse than \(10^{10}\). The comparison is with the best known classical method. No one has proved that a faster classical algorithm cannot exist, so the gap is not a proven separation.
