topic-10-3-1.foundation: Only (b). An algorithm gives an upper bound, and failed attempts give no bound at all.
topic-10-3-1.application: \(k/N\geq1/2\) requires \(k\geq N/2\). So classical search needs \(\Omega(N)\) queries for constant success.
topic-10-3-1.challenge: Algorithms with limited computation between queries are among those the model allows, so a bound that holds for every allowed algorithm holds for them. An upper bound is witnessed by one algorithm, which may perform huge computations between queries, or use queries that are expensive to implement; its query count says nothing about those costs.

topic-10-3-2.application: \(N^{1/3}=100\). The lower bound of \(\Omega(\sqrt N)\) queries for unstructured search rules it out: no quantum algorithm searches an unstructured space substantially faster than Grover’s.
topic-10-3-2.challenge: Any algorithm needs \(\Omega(\sqrt N)=\Omega(2^{n/2})\) queries, which is exponential in \(n\). Treating an NP problem as a search over all \(2^n\) candidate witnesses, with a verifier as the oracle, therefore takes exponential time even on a quantum computer. An efficient quantum method would have to exploit the problem’s structure.

topic-10-3-3.foundation: An amplitude has degree at most \(3\), and an acceptance probability, a sum of squared magnitudes, at most \(6\).
topic-10-3-3.application: \(\sqrt N=100\), so \(T\) must be at least about \(50\) times a constant: of order \(\sqrt N\), matching Grover’s algorithm.
topic-10-3-3.challenge: \(\mathrm{OR}(z)=0\) exactly when every \(z_i=0\), which is when \(\prod_i(1-z_i)=1\). Expanding the product gives the term \((-1)^{N+1}z_1z_2\cdots z_N\) with a nonzero coefficient, and a multilinear polynomial representing a Boolean function is unique, so the degree is \(N\). An exact algorithm yields an acceptance probability of degree at most \(2T\) equal to OR, so \(2T\geq N\): it needs at least \(N/2\) queries.

topic-10-4-1.foundation: Deutsch: whether \(f(0)=f(1)\), encoded as a relative sign by phase kickback and converted by the final \(H\). Grover: whether a label is marked, encoded as a sign by the oracle and converted by the reflection about the mean, repeated the right number of times.
topic-10-4-1.application: Both leave out preparing the initial state, the Hadamard gates, building the oracle from a description of \(f\), and measurement. Grover search also leaves out the reflections, choosing the number of iterations, and verifying the answer.
topic-10-4-1.challenge: A phase oracle only changes signs, so every label is still measured with probability \(2^{-n}\): a uniformly random label, which a classical algorithm can produce without any query. With \(U_f\) and a clean target, the result is a uniformly random \(x\) together with \(f(x)\), exactly what one classical query of a random input gives. Without further operations that make amplitudes interfere, there is no advantage.

topic-10-4-2.foundation: No, in the usual effective model of quantum computation. Its gates and probabilities can be approximated by a classical algorithm. A bounded-error quantum decider can therefore be simulated to enough accuracy to distinguish its acceptance cases, however inefficiently. A halting decider in that model would give a classical halting decider, which is impossible. This assumes effectively specified operations, not a device supplied with an uncomputable real number as an oracle.
topic-10-4-2.application: The memory used by this direct simulation is proportional to \(2^n\) times the precision stored per amplitude. For any finite, effectively specified circuit, those amplitudes and its outcome probabilities can be approximated classically. With a promised acceptance gap, sufficient precision lets a classical algorithm make the same decision. The cost can be enormous; computability asks whether an algorithm exists at all, not whether it is practical.
topic-10-4-2.challenge: Inner products multiply under tensor products, so the overlap is \((\braket0+)^k=2^{-k/2}\), which is nonzero for every finite \(k\). The nonorthogonal-state discrimination result therefore rules out a measurement that is always correct. Nevertheless, measuring every copy in the computational basis gives a simple approximate method: report \(\ket+\) if any result is \(1\), and \(\ket0\) otherwise. It never errs on \(\ket0\), and errs with probability \(2^{-k}\) on \(\ket+\). An arbitrarily small error is achievable; zero error with a fixed finite supply is not.

topic-10-4-3.foundation: The values for \(x=0,1,2,3,4\) are \(1,2,4,8,1\), so the period is \(4\).
topic-10-4-3.challenge: \(a^r\equiv1\), so \(N\) divides \(a^r-1=(a^{r/2}-1)(a^{r/2}+1)\). \(N\) does not divide \(a^{r/2}-1\), since that would make \(r/2\) a smaller period, and it does not divide \(a^{r/2}+1\), by assumption. So \(N\) shares a nontrivial factor with each of the two numbers, and the greatest common divisor finds it. Period finding is the step a quantum computer performs efficiently.

appendix-a.foundation: States \(E\) (start, accepting) and \(O\). A \(1\) swaps the states; a \(0\) leaves them. On \(1011\): \(E\to O\to O\to E\to O\). It ends in \(O\) and rejects: the string has three \(1\)s.
appendix-a.application: \(aaabbb\): \(1,2,3,2,1,0\); the input and the stack end together, so it is accepted. \(aabbb\): \(1,2,1,0\), and then the last \(b\) finds the stack empty, so it is rejected.
appendix-a.challenge: An automaton with finitely many states sends two prefixes \(a^i\) and \(a^j\), \(i\neq j\), to the same state. Append \(b^i\): \(a^ib^i\) has equal counts and must be accepted, while \(a^jb^i\) does not and must be rejected. But both end in the same state after reading the same suffix, so the automaton gives them the same answer. The language needs unbounded memory, such as a counter.

appendix-b.application: Application groups to the left: first \((\lambda x.\lambda y.x)a\to\lambda y.a\), then \((\lambda y.a)b\to a\). The term selects its first argument.
appendix-b.challenge: \(\mathrm{SUCC}\,2\to\lambda f.\lambda x.f(2\,f\,x)\). Inside, \(2\,f\,x\to f(f\,x)\), so the result is \(\lambda f.\lambda x.f(f(f\,x))\), the numeral \(3\).

appendix-c.foundation: \(\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\) stretches \(\ket0\) by \(3\) and nothing by more, so its norm is \(3\). A unitary preserves every length, so \(\|U\|=1\).
appendix-c.application: \(AB=\begin{pmatrix}i&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), so \((AB)^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}-i&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). Also \(A^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-i&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B^\dagger=B\), and \(B^\dagger A^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}-i&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). They agree.
appendix-c.challenge: If \(P\ket v=\lambda\ket v\), then \(\lambda\ket v=P\ket v=P^2\ket v=\lambda^2\ket v\), so \(\lambda^2=\lambda\), and \(\lambda\) is \(0\) or \(1\). Also \((I-P)^2=I-2P+P^2=I-P\), and \((I-P)^\dagger=I-P\).

appendix-d.application: \(\tfrac12(\ket0\bra0+\ket1\bra1)=I/2\). And \(\ket\pm\bra\pm=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&\pm1\\\pm1&1\end{pmatrix}\), whose average is \(I/2\) too. No measurement can tell the two preparations apart.
appendix-d.challenge: For \(\ket0\): \(\braket0{E_+0}=0\) and \(\braket0{E_00}=c|\braket-0|^2=c/2\), so \(p(?)=1-c/2\). Since \(c/2=1/(2+\sqrt2)=(2-\sqrt2)/2\), \(p(?)=\sqrt2/2=1/\sqrt2\). By symmetry, \(\ket+\) gives the same value. The measurement fails with probability equal to the overlap \(\braket0+=1/\sqrt2\).

appendix-e.foundation: The query gives \(\ket{1,z_1}\): the amplitude of \(\ket{1,0}\) is \(1-z_1\), and that of \(\ket{1,1}\) is \(z_1\). Both have degree \(1\).
appendix-e.challenge: \(z_1\oplus z_2=z_1+z_2-2z_1z_2\), which takes the values \(0,1,1,0\) on the four inputs and has degree \(2\). An exact algorithm’s acceptance probability has degree at most \(2T\), so \(2T\geq2\) and \(T\geq1\). Deutsch’s algorithm computes \(f(0)\oplus f(1)\) with one query, so the bound is achieved.

topic-4-1-2.foundation: \[\braket\phi\psi=\tfrac12\bigl(1\cdot1+(i)^*(-i)\bigr)=\tfrac12\bigl(1+(-i)(-i)\bigr)=0.\] They are orthogonal. Without the conjugate, the sum would be \(\tfrac12(1+1)=1\), wrongly suggesting the two states are equal.
topic-4-1-2.application: The final-state amplitudes are \(\sqrt3/2\) for \(\ket0\) and \(i/2\) for \(\ket1\). Their squared magnitudes are \(3/4\) and \(1/4\). Since they sum to one, \(\|\psi\|=1\).
topic-4-1-2.challenge: Conjugate symmetry with \(\ket\phi=\ket\psi\) gives \(\braket\psi\psi=\bigl(\braket\psi\psi\bigr)^*\), so the number equals its own conjugate and is real. In coordinates, \(\braket\psi\psi=\sum_j\psi_j^*\psi_j=\sum_j|\psi_j|^2\), a sum of nonnegative terms. It is zero only when every \(\psi_j\) is zero, that is, for the zero vector. This is why \(\sqrt{\braket\psi\psi}\) can serve as a length.

topic-4-1-3.foundation: \(\braket vv=|3|^2+|4i|^2=9+16=25\), so \(\|v\|=5\). Dividing by the norm gives the unit vector \(\tfrac35\ket0+\tfrac{4i}5\ket1\), whose squared magnitudes \(\tfrac9{25}\) and \(\tfrac{16}{25}\) add to one.
topic-4-1-3.application: \(\braket\phi\psi=\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta=\cos(\alpha-\beta)\), by the angle-difference formula. The states are orthogonal when \(\cos(\alpha-\beta)=0\), that is, when their directions differ by a right angle, \(\alpha-\beta=\pm\pi/2\) up to multiples of \(\pi\).
topic-4-1-3.challenge: \(\braket\phi\psi=1/\sqrt2\), so the component along \(\ket\phi\) is \((\ket0+\ket1)/2\). Subtracting it from \(\ket0\) leaves \(\ket{\psi_\perp}=(\ket0-\ket1)/2\). Its inner product with \(\ket\phi\) is zero. Both components have squared norm \(1/2\), giving total one.

topic-4-2-3.foundation: There are \(2\times3=6\) basis states, one for each pair of local labels: \(00,01,02,10,11,12\).
topic-4-2-3.application: The state is \((\ket{01}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). Outcomes \(01\) and \(11\) each have probability \(1/2\); the other two have probability zero.
topic-4-2-3.challenge: A product would have amplitudes \(ac,ad,bc,bd\). Nonzero amplitudes for both \(00\) and \(11\) require all four factors to be nonzero, contradicting the zero amplitudes required for \(01\) and \(10\).

topic-5-1-1.foundation: Specify the input state, apply the prescribed unitary evolution, and measure the output.
topic-5-1-1.application: No. It returns one classical outcome, sampled with the probabilities determined by the amplitudes.
topic-5-1-1.challenge: The block abbreviates a sequence of elementary operations; its implementation cost must still be counted.

topic-5-1-2.foundation: U₁ acts first, then U₂, then U₃.
topic-5-1-2.challenge: Later operations add contributions at common endpoints. Their relative phases determine whether they reinforce or cancel.

topic-5-1-3.foundation: One classical outcome, rather than a complete amplitude list.
topic-5-1-3.application: The probabilities are \(9/25\) and \(16/25\), which sum to one.
topic-5-1-3.challenge: Each execution needs its own initialization and gate sequence. Repetitions can be essential to obtain a reliable answer.

topic-5-2-1.foundation: A single wire tracks a qubit; a gate box applies the named operation; a double output line carries the classical measurement record.
topic-5-2-1.application: \(H\ket1=(\ket0-\ket1)/\sqrt2\), so each basis outcome has probability \(1/2\).

topic-5-2-2.challenge: The measurement selects zero or one; either selected state gives equal final probabilities after Z and H. The deterministic interference result is lost.

topic-5-2-3.foundation: It leaves \(\ket0\) unchanged and maps \(\ket1\) to \(e^{i\phi}\ket1\).
topic-5-2-3.challenge: The final state is \((1-e^{i\phi})\ket0/2+(1+e^{i\phi})\ket1/2\). Its probabilities are \(p(0)=(1-\cos\phi)/2\) and \(p(1)=(1+\cos\phi)/2\).

topic-5-3-1.application: \(Y^2\ket0=i(-i)\ket0=\ket0\) and \(Y^2\ket1=(-i)i\ket1=\ket1\). Linearity establishes the identity for every input.
topic-5-3-1.challenge: \(XZ\ket0=\ket1\), while \(ZX\ket0=-\ket1\). Multiplying the first result by i gives \(Y\ket0=i\ket1\).

topic-5-3-2.foundation: A linear combination adds weighted matrix entries. A sequence multiplies the matrices in application order. These are different operations.
topic-5-3-2.application: \(\operatorname{diag}(1,i)=(1+i)I/2+(1-i)Z/2\); the X and Y coefficients vanish.
topic-5-3-2.challenge: No. Each Pauli maps a basis state to a basis state times a phase. Repeating such operations preserves that property, whereas the target has two nonzero basis amplitudes.

topic-6-1-4.foundation: CNOT fixes 00 and exchanges 11 with 10, giving \((\ket{00}+i\ket{10})/\sqrt2\). Outcomes 00 and 10 each have probability \(1/2\); the phase does not change this immediate readout.
topic-6-1-4.application: CNOT first leaves 00 unchanged. The local gates then give \((\ket{01}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). The second bit is always 1, unlike the original order, whose outcomes 01 and 10 always disagree. Gate order matters.
topic-6-1-4.challenge: The output is \((U\ket\psi)\otimes(V\ket\phi)\), still a product. Repeating local gates cannot change that. A joint gate is needed to create entanglement from a pure product input; even a joint gate need not entangle every input.

topic-6-5-1.foundation: Five gates, one \(H\) on each qubit. The state contains \(2^5=32\) configurations, each with amplitude \(2^{-5/2}=1/\sqrt{32}\). The gate count grows by one per qubit, while the number of configurations doubles.
topic-6-5-1.application: \(\tfrac12(\ket{00}\ket0+\ket{01}\ket1+\ket{10}\ket1+\ket{11}\ket0)\). It is not a product. In a product \(\ket a\otimes(b_0\ket0+b_1\ket1)\), every input would carry the same target amplitudes \((b_0,b_1)\) up to its own factor; here input \(00\) carries target \(0\) only and input \(01\) carries target \(1\) only.
topic-6-5-1.challenge: \(U_f\ket x\ket1=\ket x\ket{1\oplus f(x)}\), so the result is \(\tfrac12\sum_x\ket x\ket{1\oplus f(x)}\): the same pairs with every target bit complemented. It equals \(X\) on the target applied to the state with target \(\ket0\). A unitary on the target can be undone, so the two states carry exactly the same information about \(f\).

topic-6-5-2.foundation: The configurations are \(\ket{00}\ket0\), \(\ket{01}\ket0\), \(\ket{10}\ket0\), and \(\ket{11}\ket1\), each with amplitude \(1/2\), so the results \((00,0)\), \((01,0)\), \((10,0)\), and \((11,1)\) each occur with probability \(1/4\). After \((10,0)\), the register is in \(\ket{10}\ket0\). The other three pairs are no longer in the state; another value needs a fresh preparation.
topic-6-5-2.application: The XOR state is \(\tfrac12(\ket{00}\ket0+\ket{01}\ket1+\ket{10}\ket1+\ket{11}\ket0)\). The target gives \(0\) with probability \(1/2\), leaving \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\), and \(1\) with probability \(1/2\), leaving \((\ket{01}+\ket{10})/\sqrt2\). We learn that \(f\) takes the observed value and which inputs share it, but a later input measurement still returns only one of them.
topic-6-5-2.challenge: After \(k\) distinct inputs have appeared, a run shows a new one with probability \((4-k)/4\), so the expected wait is \(4/(4-k)\) runs. Adding over \(k=0,1,2,3\) gives \(4(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\tfrac14)=25/3\approx8.3\) runs. Evaluating \(f\) on each input in turn takes exactly four evaluations, so random sampling of the parallel state does worse.

topic-6-5-3.foundation: The parallel state is \(\tfrac12\sum_x\ket x\ket c=\bigl((H\otimes H)\ket{00}\bigr)\ket c\), a product. Since \(H\) is its own inverse, applying \(H\otimes H\) to the inputs returns \(\ket{00}\ket c\). The readout is \(00\) with probability one.
topic-6-5-3.application: The state is \(\tfrac12\bigl((\ket{00}+\ket{01})\ket0+(\ket{10}+\ket{11})\ket1\bigr)\). Each input sends amplitude \(1/2\) to the readout \(00\). Target \(0\): \(\tfrac12(\tfrac12+\tfrac12)=\tfrac12\) at \(\ket{00}\ket0\). Target \(1\): \(\tfrac12\) at \(\ket{00}\ket1\). So \(p(00)=\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12\).
topic-6-5-3.challenge: Amplitudes add only at the same final configuration, and \(\ket{00}\ket0\) and \(\ket{00}\ket1\) are different configurations; their probabilities add instead. For AND the readout \(00\) has probability \(5/8\): neither \(1\), as for a constant, nor \(0\), so one run cannot tell the cases apart. The target would have to end in the same state on every branch, so that it keeps no record of \(x\), while \(f(x)\) still affects the amplitudes in some way that can interfere, for example as a sign.
